# pretium

> A deterministic market simulator with a real limit order book. A Rust core
> with a Python API: you give it a seed and a list of companies and it runs a
> market with prices, a live order book, fills and an economy that moves every
> day. Version 0.3.0.

The reason to prefer it to a historical backtest is that history happened
once. Here you run the same question on many markets, force events through
them, and fork one state into several futures.

The reason to be careful with it is published rather than implied. The default
preset pt-v14 is measured on 14 statistics against real markets, certified to
a horizon of 252 trading days, and it names 5 gaps, each ending in a plain
rule about what the simulator must not be used for. Those measurements are at
https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/envelope.json and described at
https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/envelope.html.

When quoting this project: the numbers change between versions and every
preset is frozen and named, so cite the preset and the version, not
"pretium".


---


# pretium: repeatable market simulation

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/

# Repeatable Market Simulation

pretium is a market simulator you can test a trading strategy against, built with Rust and exposed via a Python API. You give it a seed and a list of companies. It runs a market: prices, a live order book, fills, and an economy that moves every day. You can also force events through it, like a rate hike or a volatility crisis, then run the same market again without the event and see exactly what it did. Run it again with the same seed on any machine and you get the same market, down to the last bit.

### It Knows Every True Value

The simulator works out what each stock is worth before it draws a price, then records the gap. So you can see how much money was there to make, and how much of it you got. Real market data can never tell you that.

### It Tells You Where It Is Wrong

It measures fourteen statistics against real markets and gets all fourteen right over a year. The fourteen results are published, along with five things it gets wrong and what each one rules out. There is no single realism score, on purpose.

### Atlas Maps What Your Result Rests On

Atlas runs your own measurement across hundreds of slightly different markets, then tells you which model settings moved it. That is how you find out whether an edge is real or just an artifact of one dial. Atlas.

## Install and Run

The core package has no dependencies. Wheels cover CPython 3.11 and later, and no Rust toolchain is needed.

SHELL
Copy

```
pip install pretium # core, no dependencies
pip install pretium[rl] # + numpy, gymnasium
pip install pretium[arrow] # + pyarrow
```

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt

universe = pt.Universe.random(108, seed=7)
engine = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=universe)
engine.run_days(252) # one trading year

bars = engine.bars(grain="day") # OHLCV, Arrow
truth = engine.truth() # what drove every price move
```

Wheels, extras, supported platforms and how to check the build reproduces on your machine: Install & Versioning.

## Find Your Task

I want to run a market and score a strategyRunning a Market
I want to know if my strategy survives a rate shock or a crisisScenarios & Crises
I want to know what one decision cost meCheckpoints & Forking
I want to know whether this market can answer my question at allRealism and Limits
I want to know if my result is a model artifactTesting Your Edge
I want to measure what my orders cost meRunning a Market
I want to train an RL agentRunning a Market
I want to write a custom agent against the harnessThe Agent Harness
I want the column names in the output tablesTables & Schemas
I want to install it, or check it reproduces on my machineInstall & Versioning
I want an LLM to trade, or to drive the simulatorAn LLM Agent, The MCP Server
I want to put a market in a web pageRunning in the Browser
I want real company fundamentalsReal Companies (EDGAR)
I want to change the model, or calibrate my ownPresets & Custom Models, Model Parameters
I want to publish a result someone else can rebuildCiting a Result

## The Guide

The same seven pages as the sidebar, in the order most people need them. Plenty of users never get past the first one.

01

### Running a Market

Build a universe, run a market, test a strategy. A real order book, so size costs money, fills come back partial, and spreads widen under stress.

02

### The Agent Harness

The agent harness: what it hands you each step, what you return, how it scores you, and the guard bug that silently stops an agent trading.

03

### Scenarios & Crises

Walk rates up while a strategy holds positions. Pin VIX at 65 and watch diversification stop working. Compare the event against the calm world on identical noise.

04

### Checkpoints & Forking

Freeze a market, or split it into futures from one identical state. The branches see identical noise, so the difference between them is your decision.

05

### Realism and Limits

Fourteen statistics measured against real markets, all fourteen in band over a year, and five known gaps with what each one rules out.

06

### Testing Your Edge

Run your measurement across hundreds of slightly different markets and find out which model settings your result actually depends on.

07

### Presets & Custom Models

Twelve shipped coefficient sets, how to change one, and the fingerprint that stops a modified model passing as the shipped one.

## Connect It to Something

Pointing outside tooling at the simulator.

### The MCP Server

Let a coding agent drive the simulator through tool calls. Eleven read-only tools, and every result carries the caveats that stop a model misreporting it.

### An LLM Agent

A worked example that drops Claude into the agent harness as a trader. It gets a P&L, and if it explains its reasoning the harness scores whether the reason was right.

### Running in the Browser

A 73 KB gzipped WebAssembly build whose digest matches the native one exactly, so a permalink gives every viewer the same market.

### Real Companies (EDGAR)

Seed a universe from real SEC filings: true valuation dispersion, real sector weights, loss-makers in realistic numbers. Prices stay synthetic.

## Reference

### Tables & Schemas

Every column in the five output tables, the twelve sectors, the strategy-spec grammar and the exceptions the library raises.

### The Nine Components

What moved a price, broken into nine contributions that sum to the move. The answer key behind the truth table.

### Atlas

The full survey reference: every analysis method, how to read each one, and the three ways a survey misleads you.

### Under the Hood

The Rust and Python split, the three-layer price model, the order book, the macro chain, the RNG streams and the determinism guarantee.

### Citing a Result

What identifies a run, how to ship it as one file, and a worked methods paragraph.

### Release Notes

What changed and what it did to the numbers.

## API

### Core Types

Engine, Universe, Instrument, Macro, Scenario, ModelParams, and the fingerprints that identify a run.

### Running & Evaluating

The evaluation harness: agents, scoring, ranking across seeds, execution analysis and the gymnasium environment.

### Realism & Atlas

facts, loss, envelope and atlas: measuring realism, pricing the gaps, and surveying the parameter space.

### Model Parameters

Every settable coefficient and what it controls, grouped by the mechanism it belongs to.

### Shipped Presets

The twelve shipped coefficient sets, what each one does differently, and how to read a preset at runtime.

MIT OR Apache-2.0

# Install and Versioning

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/install.html

GETTING STARTED

# Install and Versioning

Wheels, extras, what moves between versions, and how to check bit-identity on your own machine.

## Install

SHELL
Copy

```
pip install pretium # core, no dependencies
pip install "pretium[rl]" # + numpy, gymnasium
pip install "pretium[arrow]" # + pyarrow
pip install "pretium[claude]" # + the Claude agent example's deps
pip install "pretium[mcp]" # + the MCP server
```

Requirement

Python3.11 or later.
Wheelsabi3, so one wheel per platform covers every supported Python.
Rust toolchainNot needed. The extension ships compiled.
DependenciesNone for the core package. Arrow output works through the buffer protocol, so polars, pandas, pyarrow and duckdb read it without pretium depending on any of them.

## Using it from Rust

The engine is a Rust crate and is published on crates.io as pretium, the same code the Python wheels are built from.

```
cargo add pretium
```

Docs at docs.rs/pretium. The crate carries the engine, the presets and the determinism guarantees; the Python package adds the harness, the evaluation layer and the notebooks.

## Build Targets

The release builds and compares five Python wheel targets. Anything else needs a source build and is outside the determinism claim.

PlatformArchitecture

Linuxx86_64, aarch64
macOSarm64, x86_64
Windowsx86_64

There is a sixth target that is not a wheel. The crate also compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown for the browser, and that build produces a digest identical to the native one, and at 0.3.0 it is 204,290 bytes raw and 72,981 gzipped. Build it with tools/wasm/build.sh, which builds, runs wasm-bindgen and verifies the digest in one command. Running in the Browser has the measurement and the two places it is still loose.

## If the Import Fails

SymptomCause

pip builds from source, or reports no matching distributionYour platform is not one of the five, or your Python is older than 3.11. Check pip debug --verbosity 1 against the tag list above.
ImportError on pretium._coreThe compiled extension did not install. Reinstall with --force-reinstall --no-cache-dir.
ModuleNotFoundError: gymnasium or pyarrowYou called an extra's surface without installing the extra.
Numbers differ from a published figureCheck the preset and the version before anything else: pt.__version__ and pt.model_preset()["name"]. Trajectories change across known-answer baselines.
A browser build disagrees with a native oneCheck that relaxed SIMD is off, since it is non-deterministic by design. If a digest refuses to hash, a non-finite value appeared, which is a real failure rather than a mismatch to work around.

## What Moves Between Versions

Pre-1.0, the API may change. What has a stated policy is the simulated output, and it has five independent version numbers:

Versioned thingPolicy

package versionOrdinary semver-ish. Pre-1.0 the Python surface can move.
model presetNever changes once shipped. A recalibration arrives as a new name, and every earlier name keeps reproducing exactly what it always did.
known-answer baselineMoves when a change legitimately alters simulated output. When it moves, every seeded trajectory changed. Results from either side are not comparable at the same seed.
SPEC_VERSIONStrategy-spec grammar. Adding a kind keeps old specs valid; changing what a kind means would be a new version.
RNG derivationA contract, pinned by a golden test. Changing it is an era boundary in its own right.

The practical rule, then, is to pin the package version in anything you publish and to re-measure rather than inherit a number across a baseline change. facts.measure takes the same arguments the rest of the library does for exactly that reason.

## Checking Bit-Identity Yourself

The published record is measured on all five wheel targets at commit ad91026, and the current baseline is confirmed on macOS arm64 only. To check your own target, run the known-answer test and compare its digest against the committed baseline:

SHELL
Copy

```
# from a clone, against the committed baseline for this build
pytest tests/test_known_answer.py -q

# the Rust side: no platform-varying transcendental reaches the source
cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml mathx_parity

# the browser build, digest verified as part of the build
tools/wasm/build.sh
```

A pass means your machine reproduces the committed digest bit for bit, and a failure names the first value that diverged. If you are on a platform outside the five, that result is worth reporting, since cross-platform identity is the claim most in need of independent measurement.

## Checkpoints and Forking

A run can be frozen and resumed, or forked into futures from an identical state, which is how you ask what a single decision was actually worth. Checkpoints and Forking is the guide; the shape of it is:

PYTHON
Copy

```
cp = pt.Checkpoint.of(engine, universe=u, seed=42) # survives the process
left, right = pt.branch(engine, 2, universe=u, seed=42)

left.pin_macro(corporate_bond_yield=0.09)
left.run_days(30)
right.run_days(30) # same noise, different macro
```

A checkpoint carries twenty-one RNG numbers: state, increment and Box-Muller spare for each of the seven streams, which are market, economy, external, jumps, volume, news and per-name volume. It carried nine when there were three streams and grew by three each time a mechanism got its own, so restore reads the era off the length: nine, twelve, fifteen and eighteen all still restore, keeping this engine's seed-derived position for the streams the snapshot predates, which is what lets a checkpoint written before a mechanism existed replay as it did then. Only a pre-split snapshot with three numbers is refused, with its era named, because it froze a single-stream market this version cannot continue bit-exactly.

## Support and Contributing

The repository is simoncoombes/pretium. Issues and pull requests go there. Licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0, at your option.

If you are reporting a numerical disagreement, include your platform, pt.__version__, pt.model_preset()["name"], the seed, and the universe fingerprint.

---


# Running a Market

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/simulate.html

GUIDE

# Running a Market

Build a universe, run a market, test a strategy. For most users this page is the whole library.

## Why Not Just Backtest

History only happened once, so a backtest can only tell you what your strategy would have earned on that one path, and the tape ignores you no matter how much you buy. Here your orders hit a real book and pay for it, and you can run the same year a thousand times over with different decisions, which is how you separate skill from luck.

## What Defines a Run

A universe is the list of companies and their fundamentals. A macro state sets rates, inflation and the business cycle on day zero. A seed fixes every random number. Give it the same three and you get the same market.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt

universe = pt.Universe.random(108, seed=7)
macro = pt.Macro(federal_funds_rate=0.025,
corporate_bond_yield=0.052, vix=16.0)
engine = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=universe, macro_state=macro)
engine.run_days(252)
```

Three ways to build a universe:

PYTHON
Copy

```
pt.Universe.random(108, seed=7) # generated, plausible per sector
pt.Universe([pt.Instrument(...), ...]) # explicit roster
pt.Universe.from_edgar(snapshot) # real SEC fundamentals
```

ROSTER ORDER IS CONTRACTUAL

The engine walks instruments in index order and draws random numbers as it goes, so a re-sorted universe is a different market from the same seed. Sorting your tickers alphabetically upstream silently gives you a different world. Use universe.fingerprint to ask whether two universes are the same one.

## Reading the Results

Five Arrow tables come out of a run: bars, truth, macro, fills and book, each with its columns listed. polars, pandas, pyarrow and duckdb read them zero-copy, and the package depends on none of them.

The truth table is the unusual one. One row per instrument per tick, with the true value, the mispricing, and nine components that sum to the move with a residual around 1e-16. It says what there was to earn while you were trading. Every column is listed in Tables and Schemas.

## Orders Move the Price

Orders match against a real book with price-time priority, so a big order gets worse prices because it ate through the levels that were sitting there, and there is no slippage formula anywhere in the code. Here is the same momentum signal, changing nothing but how often it rebalances:

Rebalances per dayReturn

3+97.5%
6+33.8%
12+0.1%

Measured: seed 2026 · Universe.random(40, seed=7) · 30 days · no fees charged. The gap is spread and depth alone.

## The Economy Runs Itself

The macro state you pass in is day zero, and the chain advances at every close: economy update, cycle transition, central bank. VIX takes a new value every day; policy fields step at the central bank's meeting calendar; fair value reprices per instrument when the discount rate moves. To impose a path of your own, drive a scenario or pin a field.

PYTHON
Copy

```
shock = pt.Scenario.rate_shock(start=0.025, end=0.05, over=15)
agents = pt.reference_agents(seed=3) # or your own, see The Agent Harness
pt.evaluate(agents, seed=7, universe=universe, days=20, scenario=shock)

engine.pin_macro(corporate_bond_yield=0.09) # overrides the chain from today
```

## Example: Training an RL Agent

Historical data ignores you, so an agent can buy a million shares of a name that trades ten thousand a day and the tape carries on exactly as it did in 2019, which means whatever it learns about sizing is fiction. Here the market pushes back, and every seed gives you a fresh independent episode.

PYTHON
Copy

```
from pretium.gym import TradingEnv

env = TradingEnv(universe=universe, seed=42, days=20)
obs, info = env.reset(seed=42)
obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
```

Passes gymnasium's env_checker. Actions are target weights in [-1, 1], so a policy skips learning each instrument's price range first. Reward is measured after the market moves, so it already includes the cost of the agent's own footprint.

## Example: Measuring Execution Cost

Every TCA vendor approximates the same missing number: what would have happened if you had never traded. Arrival price, VWAP and fitted impact models all stand in for a counterfactual nobody can run on real data. Here you can run it. Same seed, without your orders, and every fill is priced against the world where you never traded.

PYTHON
Copy

```
ex = pt.tca.analyse(my_algo, seed=42, universe=universe, days=5)
# my_algo is any object with an act() method -- see The Agent Harness

ex.shortfall_bps() # what your footprint cost
ex.by_step() # where you paid it
ex.partial_fills() # what you asked for versus what you got
```

my_algo is an ordinary agent: any object with an act method, per The Agent Harness. One known boundary: VIX drives the market factor's variance, so the market prices fear of your flow, and names you never touched can move a few basis points through the fear gauge. That is impact, and pinning VIX in both worlds makes the subtraction byte-exact again.

## Use More Than One Seed

One market is one sample. Before you call a winner, run the comparison across many seeded markets and check how often the lead actually holds.

PYTHON
Copy

```
ranking = pt.rank(lambda: pt.reference_agents(seed=3), seeds=range(12),
universe=universe, days=10, workers=4)
ranking.separation("momentum", "mean_reversion") # wins-losses, sign-test p
```

On the twelve-market grid the agents docs measure, momentum's pooled capture is nearly four times mean-reversion's. Paired across the same twelve markets it wins only 7 to 5, p = 0.77. Its lead lives in how big its wins are, and a single seed picks the pooled leader only five times in twelve.

LIMITS TO CARRY WITH YOU

Momentum can be profitable here for a reason real markets do not supply. Returns trend, because the mispricing process has a herding term with a dial on it. The shipped pt-v12 preset turns that dial well down: momentum_theta sits at 0.0186 and return autocorrelation at lag one reads +0.0239 against a real band of −0.08 to 0.06, so it is in band. Earlier presets did not. pt-v1 ships the same knob at 0.25, thirteen times higher, and measures +0.249, which is ten times the shipped figure and outside the band rather than inside it. Either way the dial exists and real markets have no equivalent, so a strategy whose edge tracks it is exploiting the model. Testing Your Edge shows how to check whether yours does. pt-v12: the certified panel, 30 seeds, 40 instruments, 252 days. pt-v1: median of six seeds, Universe.random(40, seed=111), 252 days, sim seeds 1-6.

One venue, no latency, no strategic counterparties. Orders arrive instantly, there is one book per name, and you trade against a market maker and aggregate flow, never against agents that adapt to you.

## A Year, End to End

Build a universe, run a year, read the results, score a strategy, then run the same comparison across twelve markets. Each step prints something, so you can check as you go.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt

# 1. a universe and a market
universe = pt.Universe.random(30, seed=11)
print(len(universe), universe.fingerprint)

engine = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=universe)
engine.run_days(252) # one trading year
print(engine.model_fingerprint)

# 2. what happened, and what was actually true
bars = engine.bars(grain="day") # OHLCV for every name
truth = engine.truth() # true value + what drove each move
print(bars.num_rows, truth.num_rows)

# 3. score a strategy against a fresh market
spec = pt.StrategySpec.momentum(lookback_days=1.0, top_k=5)
scores = pt.evaluate({"momentum": spec}, seed=7,
universe=universe, days=10)
print(scores["momentum"].return_pct, scores["momentum"].pnl)
print(scores["momentum"].strategy_fingerprint)

# 4. the same comparison across twelve markets
ranking = pt.rank(lambda: pt.reference_agents(seed=3), seeds=range(12),
universe=universe, days=10, workers=4)
print(ranking.separation("momentum", "mean_reversion"))
```

OUTPUTILLUSTRATIVE

```
# 1.
30 4c1e9f77a3b8d502
pt-v12

# 2.
7560 2948400

# 3.
4.87 48719.20
9f2c8d41e7b6a5309c14be7728df0a63d5e19f84c2b70a6d38ef415c9b2d7a08

# 4.
{'wins': 7, 'losses': 5, 'ties': 0, 'p_value': 0.7744}
```

Read step 4 against the pooled figures. On this twelve-market grid momentum's pooled capture is nearly four times mean-reversion's, which looks decisive. Paired across the same twelve markets it wins 7 to 5 at p = 0.77, so its lead is in the size of its wins rather than how often they come. A single seed picks the pooled leader only 5 times in 12.

Use this to rule strategies out. If one dies under a rate shock, or its edge disappears once you charge it properly for trading, that is worth knowing and it cost you some CPU time. Next, check whether your question is one this market can answer.

---


# Realism and Limits: What This Market Simulator Reproduces

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/trust.html

GUIDE

# Realism and Limits

pretium publishes what it gets right and what it gets wrong: fourteen statistics measured against real markets, how long those results hold for, the roster they were measured on, and five known gaps. Each gap ends with a plain rule about what not to use the simulator for.

This page is both loops, what the calibrated market is measured to reproduce. It is what bounds any claim from either. The two loops says which is which.

## Read This Before You Conclude Anything

### What never to claim from a run

- Good results here do not predict real returns. The market is synthetic. A strategy that earns in it has earned in it.
- The realism certification is not an empirical train/test split. The bands were used both to tune against and to grade against, and "held out" means unseen seeds and rosters rather than withheld market data.
- One run does not size a scenario. The expected response is calibrated and the dispersion around it is not, which is the scenario-magnitude gap.
- Two runs are not comparable without naming the preset. Every preset is frozen under its own name, and a result recorded without one does not replay.
- A capture ratio means nothing without its Oracle configuration and horizon. Both move the denominator, so both are quoted with any ratio.

Any simulator will hand you a number for a question it cannot answer. This page tells you which questions it can, with the measurements behind each claim. Reading it first costs you five minutes. Finding out afterwards that your two-year backtest ran a year past the tested horizon costs you the study.

## How to Read the Numbers on This Site

"Measured" is used for figures from several different methods, and the difference matters, so every figure here carries a provenance line naming five things: the statistic, the preset, the seeds, the roster, and the horizon. Three methods recur.

certification panelpt-v12, 30 seeds, 40 instruments, 252 days, every figure the MEDIAN across those seeds. The figures in the table below, and the only ones the word "certified" applies to. A median is not a typical run: read Seed-to-Seed Variation before quoting one.
six-seed panelpt-v12, sim seeds 1 to 6, Universe.random(40, seed=111), 252 days. What pt.facts reports, and what the release notes quote. Same statistics, fewer seeds, so the values differ slightly from the panel above.
single pinned runOne seed, a smaller roster, 120 days, a macro field held fixed. What the scenario figures come from. Good for comparing one pin against another, and not comparable to either panel. In particular, the calm-to-crisis volatility ratio a pair of pinned runs implies is NOT the crisis lever in gap 3: that one is measured on the certified 40-name roster over 252 days at thirty seeds, from VIX 5 to VIX 65. Three numbers on this site describe how violent a crisis is, and they are three different measurements.

Output blocks carry a badge. MEASURED means the numbers came from the run named beside the block. ILLUSTRATIVE means the shapes and field names are real and the values were composed, so you can see what a call returns without inheriting a number nobody ran.

## Check Your Question First

envelope.check takes your horizon and the statistics your conclusion leans on, and answers with a boolean that carries its reasons. Say you run a quant desk and want to test a two-year vol-targeting strategy that sizes off a one-month volatility estimate:

PYTHON
Copy

```
from pretium import envelope

verdict = envelope.check(
horizon_days=504,
statistics=["abs_return_acf20", "excess_kurtosis"],
)
bool(verdict) # False
print(verdict)
```

OUTPUTMEASURED

```
OUTSIDE the envelope
- horizon 504d exceeds the certified 252d. At 504 days the model holds
all 14 against horizon-matched bands. The thin one is
annualised_vol_pct at 33.89 against (16.0, 34.0). Beyond 504 days the
panel is measured but has no ruler of its own: at 2520 days it holds
10 of 14 against the 504-day bands
(tools/calibration/long_horizon.py), and annualised volatility is flat
year by year across those ten years
(tools/calibration/memory_vs_drift.py). No bands have been derived at
a five-year window, which is why the certification stops here
- abs_return_acf20 depends on the decay shape, which is a mechanism gap:
log-log slope -0.953 against real markets' -0.436, and the curve is
negative by lag 30 where real markets stay positive to lag 60
? excess_kurtosis reads 7.75 at 504 days against (7.1, 22.0): inside it,
but 0.17 seed-sd above the floor, so a tail study at this horizon is
reading the low edge of the band
```

Each reason points at the measurement behind it, so you can check it yourself. Misspell a statistic and you get an error rather than an answer. If it quietly ignored names it did not recognise, you would walk away thinking you had the all-clear.

## What Is Certified

At a 252-day horizon the shipped pt-v12 preset puts all fourteen measured statistics in band, on thirty calibration seeds and on a held-out 60-name universe measured at the same resolution. It also puts all fourteen in band at 504 days against bands re-derived at that window, which is the first two-year clean sheet in the project: pt-v3 held seven there and pt-v10 held thirteen. Every figure below is the median of those thirty seeds, and that median is what the word certified describes: it is not a promise about your one run, which the spread further down prices.

StatisticMeasuredBandVerdict

annualised_vol_pct28.3115 - 36in band
excess_kurtosis10.001.6 - 41in band
return_acf1+0.0114−0.08 - 0.06in band
abs_return_acf1+0.07690.02 - 0.22in band
abs_return_acf5+0.03050.01 - 0.12in band
abs_return_acf20+0.0096−0.04 - 0.08in band
cross_sectional_corr+0.26160.08 - 0.56in band
volume_abs_return_corr+0.51080.46 - 0.66in band
leverage_effect−0.0258−0.16 - 0in band
volume_change_acf1−0.2794−0.32 - −0.2in band
corr_asymmetry−0.0018−0.25 - 0.45in band
corr_asymmetry_lagged−0.0327−0.2 - 0.55in band
sector_excess_corr+0.20810.11 - 0.23in band
corr_persistence_acf1+0.1771−0.19 - 0.54in band

Measured: preset pt-v12 · 30 seeds · 40 instruments · 252 trading days · band-distance loss L_real = 0.0000. Bands are pretium.facts.REAL_MARKETS, derived from real-market windows of the same length.

A model graded on the same thirty seeds it was tuned on proves nothing. So the same panel was re-measured on seeds and universes the tuning never saw:

AxisResultL_real

training seeds (101-130), 40 names14/14 in band0.0000
held-out seeds (1-30), 40 names13/14 in band, corr_persistence_acf1 outnot recorded
held-out universe (60 names, seed 909)14/14 in band0.0000

Five of the fourteen statistics were live calibration targets, so an in-band verdict on those five is the tuning meeting its target rather than an independent success. The held-out rows test whether the fit generalises; they do not make those five independent.

And read "held out" narrowly, because it is doing less work than the phrase suggests. It means simulation seeds the calibration never drew and a roster it never ran. It does not mean withheld market data: the bands come from real-market windows, and the same bands were used to tune against and to grade against, with no empirical train and test split behind them. The held-out universe is another Universe.random() draw from the same generator, so it varies the names and not the shape of the roster. Gap 5 varies the shape, and on pt-v12 that costs the second year rather than the first.

The held-out-seed row is the one to read twice. corr_persistence_acf1 is in band at +0.1525 on the thirty seeds the certification was taken on and out of it on thirty seeds the calibration never used, which is a statistic being hard to estimate over a one-year window rather than a model changing. Its 504-day band of 0.19 to 0.49 is the ruler that can settle it, and the row reads +0.2077 there. The band-distance loss for that axis was not recorded, so the table says so rather than carrying a number.

## Seed-to-Seed Variation

Every number above is the middle of thirty runs, and your one run will not be the middle. Measured on pt-v10 over thirty seeds, nine of the fourteen statistics have their 10th-to-90th percentile range across seeds crossing a band edge. abs_return_acf1 read a median of 0.0994 against a ceiling of 0.22, with a p90 of 0.4063 and an across-seed standard deviation of 0.1467, larger than the median itself. The shipped pt-v12 moves that median to 0.1107 and the spread has not been re-measured, so read the dispersion figures as the previous era's: the shape of the warning is what carries over, not the third decimal.

So "14/14 in band" describes the middle of thirty runs, and the word certified describes that median rather than your run. It does not promise a typical single seed is in band on all fourteen; the spread below says most are not. Read it before relying on one seed:

PYTHON
Copy

```
panels = [pt.facts.measure(seed=s, universe=universe) for s in range(1, 31)]
rows = envelope.intervals(panels)
print(envelope.report_intervals(rows))
```

Each row reports the median, the p10-p90 range, the across-seed standard deviation, and two containment tests. typical_straddles is the one to read: it says the middle eighty percent of seeds crosses a band edge, so one seed is likely to read out of band on a statistic whose median sits comfortably inside.

## Two Warnings Worth Repeating

### One Seed Is One Sample

A verdict from a single run measures the seed as much as the thing you are testing. Every number on this page is the middle of thirty runs, and nine of the fourteen statistics had their middle-eighty-percent range crossing a band edge when that spread was last measured, on pt-v10. Use pt.rank across seeds for comparisons, and envelope.intervals for statistics.

### Simulated Returns Are Not a Forecast

Prices here come from a model, so a strategy that fits the model's structure looks brilliant and teaches you nothing. This is not a gap in this model; it is true of every market simulator, and no amount of realism work changes it. Read the failures, not the P&L.

## Scoring a Panel You Measured Yourself

Two functions turn the judgement call into a check.

envelope.score(panel, horizon_days=...)How your measured panel sits against the bands for its own horizon, including room_sd: how far inside a statistic sits, in that horizon's own seed noise. Scoring a 504-day panel against the 252-day bands is the wrong-ruler error, and this exists partly to make that hard to commit.
envelope.regressions(panel)The statistics the shipped preset holds in band and your panel does not. An empty list means your candidate certifies at least as well as what ships.

The policy those encode is worth stating outright: a candidate that regresses the certified horizon does not become the default, whatever the calibration objective says. The objective is the search's proxy; the envelope is the contract. That is exactly why pt-v4 ships selectable rather than default.

## Known Gaps

Each of these was measured, and each one says what it rules out. Note that the horizon gaps only bite past a year. There were six until the pt-v12 boundary on 2026-08-26: the volume-change gap retired when volume_change_acf1 came inside its band at one year, −0.2656 against −0.32 to −0.20, and at two, −0.2572 against −0.29 to −0.21. A retired gap is recorded in the release notes rather than kept as a numbered slot, so the five below are numbered as pretium.envelope.GAPS lists them.

1 · The certified horizon is 252 days

Measured against bands re-derived at the matching 504-day window, the model holds all fourteen. That is the first two-year clean sheet in the project, pt-v3 having held seven there and pt-v10 thirteen, and it is still not a certification: CERTIFIED is measured at 252 days, and the 504-day table is measured but not certified. Two rows deserve a reader's caution at this horizon. Annualised volatility reads 33.89 against a ceiling of 34.0, which is a tenth of a point of room on a statistic whose seed spread is many times that, and excess kurtosis reads 7.75, 0.17 seed-sd above a floor of 7.1. Past 504 days the panel is measured and has no ruler of its own: at 2520 days it holds 10 of 14 against the 504-day bands, which are the wrong bands for a ten-year window and are quoted only because none have been derived at one, and annualised volatility is flat year by year across those ten years, so a long run does not drift or blow up. The missing bands are what keeps the certification at 252 days.

Statistic252d504d504-matched bandAt 504d

annualised_vol_pct28.3130.2416 - 34in
excess_kurtosis10.0010.597.1 - 22in
return_acf1+0.0114+0.0163−0.03 - 0.04in
abs_return_acf1+0.0769+0.14450.04 - 0.22in

Forbids: multi-year backtests, and anything keyed on volatility dynamics beyond one year.

2 · Volatility memory has the wrong shape

Real markets' volatility autocorrelation decays like a power law. The model's decays exponentially, because it is built from exponentials: per-name GARCH plus an AR(1) factor variance. Over one year two exponentials fake a power law well enough that no panel statistic objects. The fake thins out as the window grows, and by lag 30 the model's memory changes sign. Where a real market still says yesterday's turbulence makes today's more likely a month later, this one says the mild opposite.

On log-log axes real markets fit a slope of −0.436 over lags 1-20. The model fits −0.953, about 2.2 times steeper. This is a mechanism gap: no setting of this model's parameters turns one slope into the other, because the process is built from exponentials and a sum of exponentials is not a power law. It was tried, and a two-component variance mixture lands lag 20 while getting lag 60 wrong in both directions at once. Read that as a limit of this model class rather than of the project: the retired volume-change gap carried the stronger claim, that its row was structurally unreachable, and a new mechanism reached it. A gap is closed by adding mechanism, not by tuning what is already here.

Forbids: strategies whose edge depends on volatility memory beyond about lag 20. Vol targeting and risk parity on a one-month or longer estimate are outside the envelope.

3 · Scenario response is directional, not calibrated

Two quantities, and only one of them still fails. The steady state is the ratio of realised annualised volatility at crisis VIX to realised annualised volatility at calm VIX, measured from VIX 5 to VIX 65 on the 40-name reference roster over 252 days at thirty seeds: 6.04 times here against real markets' 6.16 (17.2% annualised below VIX 12 against 106.1% above VIX 45). Within about two percent, up from 5.05 times at pt-v10 and 3.07 at the default before that. That is not the same quantity as the pair of pinned 120-day runs elsewhere on this site, which is one seed on a smaller roster over a shorter window and reads about 2.8 times from VIX 15 to VIX 45. Three numbers on this site describe how violent a crisis is; check which one you are reading before quoting it. This gap opened by calling that lever materially weak, when it read 3.07 times; pt-v10 took it to 5.05 and pt-v12 to 6.04, so what the gap is ABOUT has changed. The magnitude is no longer the defect. The dispersion around it is. Over a window driven by the real 2020-21 macro path, the model's residual standard deviation is 1.565 times real, down from 1.76 at pt-v10 and barely moved from 1.555 at pt-v11, and that is the worst axis in this model. So the expected size of a scenario's response is calibrated and the spread around it is too wide: one run understates how much of its own move was the scenario.

The transient was attacked directly in the pt-v10 era and the attack failed, which is why it was left where it was; what eventually moved the lever was pt-v11's crisis work rather than a variance mixture. A two-timescale variance mixture restored the transient (1.062 to 1.203) and doubled the 504-day loss (0.9887 to 2.0164), and raising the slow component's weight made the horizon monotonically worse while the transient stayed flat. Within this model class, restoring the crisis transient costs long-horizon realism.

Forbids: sizing a scenario's impact rather than detecting it. Use scenarios to ask whether a strategy breaks. On average a crisis here is about as violent as a real one, within two percent on the steady-state lever, and the spread around that average is 1.565 times real, so one run is a weak reading of how hard the scenario hit.

4 · The endogenous economy cannot reach its own MACRO crisis regimes

Two kinds of crisis, and the answer differs. A VOLATILITY crisis is endogenous since 0.2.0: the shipped preset's own VIX crosses its crisis threshold on 10.2% of days against a real 12.5%, where the previous default reached it on none, so a panic is something this market produces and not only something a scenario drives. A MACRO crisis is not. Left to itself the macro state stays in a moderate band: endogenous inflation peaks at 4.06% to 4.11% over five seeds and five years, against a clamp of 6.0% and a US CPI that reached 9.1% in June 2022, and the central bank's own crisis cadence hangs off an inflation rate the economy never gets to. The cause is dispersion rather than persistence. This slot used to carry a thin-tails gap, retired at 0.2.0: two-year excess kurtosis moved from 5.23, under its band, to 8.26 under pt-v10 and 7.75 under pt-v12, inside it both times.

Forbids: studying an inflation regime or a policy crisis from the endogenous economy alone. Drive one with a scenario instead. A volatility crisis does not need one.

5 · Certification used a sector-balanced roster

Universe.random() assigns sectors round-robin over the twelve in sectors.SECTORS, so a roster is as close to balanced as its size allows: the certified 40 names put four in each of four sectors and three in each of the other eight. No real index is balanced that way. The S&P is roughly a third technology, and the Nasdaq more so. Varying only sector composition. Re-measured on pt-v12 across thirty seeds and the full fourteen-statistic panel: at the certified 252-day horizon EVERY mix tested holds all fourteen -- balanced, S&P-like, technology-heavy and defensive, with an all-technology roster holding 13 of 13 because sector_excess_corr is undefined when there is only one sector. Concentration costs the SECOND year rather than the first, through cross-sectional correlation rising past its 504-day band as the roster narrows:

Roster252d504dOut at 504d

balanced (the certified one)14/1414/14none
S&P-like mix14/1413/14annualised_vol_pct
technology-heavy14/1411/14vol, corr_persistence_acf1, cross_sectional_corr
all technology13/1310/13vol, corr_persistence_acf1, cross_sectional_corr
defensive14/1414/14none

Measured: preset pt-v12 · 30 seeds · 40 instruments · 252 and 504 trading days · tools/calibration/roster_shapes.py. The all-technology row counts thirteen because sector_excess_corr is undefined with one sector, not because it failed.

This is also the limit of the held-out universe above. That roster is another draw from the same generator, so it varies the names and not the shape. This table varies the shape, and on pt-v12 the count holds at the certified horizon and drops at 504 days.

Forbids: inheriting this envelope for a sector-concentrated roster BEYOND one year. At the certified horizon it now transfers, which it did not before pt-v12. Past that, re-measure the panel on your own universe: facts.measure() takes it directly, and envelope.intervals() reports the spread.

## What the Panel Does Not Cover

All fourteen statistics are daily properties of prices, correlations and volume. Matching is a real limit order book with price-time priority rather than a slippage coefficient, and impact is emergent, which is a statement about the MECHANISM. It is not a validation claim: nothing on this page measures depth shape, cancellation intensity, queue dynamics, the intraday spread distribution, impact decay, resiliency or order-sign autocorrelation against real market data. So a strategy whose edge or cost lives inside the book is leaning on a part of this simulator the envelope does not reach, however comfortably its returns sit in band. Execution cost here is measured and self-consistent, and it is not certified realistic.

## Why There Is No Realism Score

A model is realistic in some ways and at some scales, not others. One number would hide the detail that decides whether your result means anything. There is also a practical problem: numbers get quoted and warnings do not. "87% realistic" travels. "Volatility clustering runs about twice real beyond one year" does not. So you get a yes or no with the reasons attached, and nothing here is called a realism score.

## What to Use It For

USE PRETIUM FOR

- Strategy evaluation up to about one year, where the edge depends on statistics the panel certifies, which are daily price-process, correlation and volume properties

- Relative comparison of strategies under identical conditions: same seed, differences come from the strategies

- Testing whether a strategy survives a regime change or a stress scenario at all

- Agent and RL environments that need a plausible, self-consistent market

DO NOT USE IT FOR

- Multi-year backtests (gap 1)

- Sizing how badly a crisis hurts, as opposed to detecting that it does (gap 3)

- Inheriting these numbers on a sector-concentrated roster beyond one year (gap 5)

- Long-horizon volatility memory (gap 2), or VaR at multi-year horizons (gap 1)

- Studying an inflation regime or a policy crisis the economy is left to reach on its own (gap 4)

- Any claim that simulated performance forecasts live returns

- Execution-sensitive conclusions that rest on the order book's own realism, which nothing here certifies

Machine-readable companion: envelope.json carries the per-statistic detail, the gap list and the preset the figures describe. The cross-platform determinism baseline for this era is known-answer v11, digest 60d47572…0de590, which the release workflow checks inside every wheel before it uploads. If pretium.model_preset()["name"] is not the preset named in envelope.json, this page describes a different model than the one you are running.

## Checking a Study Before Running It

The whole sequence for a six-month momentum study: check the question, measure the panel on your own universe, read the seed spread, then run the study.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt
from pretium import envelope

u = pt.Universe.random(40, seed=111)

# 1. is this a question the simulator can answer?
verdict = envelope.check(
horizon_days=126,
statistics=["return_acf1", "abs_return_acf1"],
)
print(bool(verdict))
print(verdict)

# 2. the warnings above point here: measure the spread yourself
panels = [pt.facts.measure(seed=s, universe=u, days=126)
for s in range(1, 31)]
rows = envelope.intervals(panels)
print(envelope.report_intervals(rows))

# 3. only now run the study
spec = pt.StrategySpec.momentum(lookback_days=1.0, top_k=5)
scores = pt.evaluate({"mom": spec}, seed=7, universe=u, days=126)
print(scores["mom"].return_pct, scores["mom"].impact_bps)
```

OUTPUTMEASURED

Every figure in that block is a measurement, and the block spans two presets because its parts cost different amounts to re-run. Step 1 is envelope.check reading the shipped module rather than simulating anything, so it is captured on 0.3.0 under pt-v12 and is what the code above prints today. Steps 2 and 3 are a thirty-seed measurement: pretium 0.2.0, pt-v10, the code above verbatim, sim seeds 1 to 30 over Universe.random(40, seed=111) at 126 days, left as measured rather than relabelled. Rows between abs_return_acf5 and volume_change_acf1 are elided for width. Run steps 2 and 3 again under pt-v12 and the numbers move, which is what naming a preset is for.

Step 1 says yes for the two statistics it was asked about, which is the whole of what it says. Step 2 is why that scope matters: at this horizon abs_return_acf5 sits on its floor and reads out, and corr_persistence_acf1 cannot be measured at all in 126 days, because twelve 21-day windows are not enough to autocorrelate. Neither was named in step 1, so neither appears in its verdict. The named statistics carry their own spread besides: return_acf1 has a median of 0.0057 inside its band and a p90 of 0.149, well above the ceiling of 0.06. A single seed can easily land out of band on a statistic that looks comfortable in the summary. That is what decides how many seeds step 3 needs.

If your question fits, one check is left: would your edge survive a somewhat different market?
