# Testing Your Edge

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/interrogate.html

GUIDE

# Testing Your Edge

A backtest runs one market, so it cannot tell you what your result rests on. Atlas runs hundreds of slightly different markets and shows you which model settings moved your number, what shape the effect had, and what trade-offs exist.

## When You Need This

You tested a strategy and it looks good. Before you rely on it, ask whether the edge would still be there if the market were a bit different. Atlas answers that by running your measurement across hundreds of variations and showing which settings your result tracks.

Atlas does not optimise anything. survey measures, the analysis methods describe, and there is no target, no gradient and no best vector. Most users never need it. You need it for this second-order question, and for calibration work.

## Example: Testing a Momentum Edge

A researcher has a momentum agent that does well on the shipped preset, and wants to know whether the edge lives in one corner of the model. The session below moves three parameters, measures the agent at 500 points, and asks the table what the Sharpe depends on.

PYTHON
Copy

```
from pretium import atlas
import pretium as pt

universe = pt.Universe.random(40, seed=111)

axes = atlas.axes_for(
["market_factor_sigma", "garch_alpha", "momentum_theta"],
ranges={"momentum_theta": (0.0, 0.4)}, # override any default box
)

def measure(vector):
model = pt.ModelParams.from_preset("pt-v3", **vector)
scores = pt.evaluate({"mine": MyAgent()}, seed=7,
universe=universe, model=model)
return {"return_pct": scores["mine"].return_pct,
"impact_bps": scores["mine"].impact_bps}

s = atlas.survey(axes, measure, samples=500)
s.save("survey.json") # measure once, ask many questions later
```

Then interrogate the table:

PYTHON
Copy

```
s.sensitivity("return_pct") # which parameters move it, ranked
s.profile("momentum_theta", "return_pct") # what shape the effect has
s.pareto({"return_pct": "max", "impact_bps": "min"})
print(s.explain("return_pct"))
```

How to read the answers. If momentum_theta dominates the sensitivity ranking, the edge rides the mispricing herding term, the same term that made pt-v1 read +0.249 at lag one and that pt-v3 turns down to a measured +0.0375. That edge is an artifact of the model and will not transfer. If the return is flat across all three ranges then the edge is at least robust to the market being somewhat different, which is the most a simulator can say for it.

MyAgent here is any object with an act method (see The Agent Harness), and measure_with_seed(vector, seed) is the same measurement taking an explicit seed. You write the measure function yourself, so Atlas works for any question: realism statistics, a Sharpe, a fill rate, an agent's score. They are all the same shape.

## Confirming on Fresh Seeds

A survey runs at screening resolution: few seeds per point, so the map stays affordable. Good enough to rank candidates, not good enough to believe one. Anything the map surfaces gets re-measured on disjoint seed blocks before it is believed:

PYTHON
Copy

```
s.confirm(candidate, baseline, measure_with_seed,
seed_blocks=[range(201, 231), range(301, 331)])
```

confirm refuses to run on seeds that overlap the survey's. The full story of why, with the reversal that motivated it, is in the Atlas reference, along with every method, the failure modes, and what a survey cannot tell you.

## Tracing an Edge to One Dial

The clearest edge-that-does-not-transfer in this library, measured end to end. Momentum agents profit here partly because returns trend, and the trendiness is one dial: momentum_theta, the herding coefficient. Survey it and watch your edge track it.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt
from pretium import atlas

universe = pt.Universe.random(40, seed=111)
spec = pt.StrategySpec.momentum(lookback_days=1.0, top_k=5)

# 1. pick the axes. momentum_theta is the herding knob; the other two
# are volatility, included so the answer is not one-dimensional.
axes = atlas.axes_for(
["momentum_theta", "garch_alpha", "market_factor_sigma"],
ranges={"momentum_theta": (0.0, 0.4)},
)

# 2. check the plan before spending anything on it
for v in atlas.plan(axes, samples=256)[:3]:
print(v)

# 3. measure your own outcome AND the statistic you suspect drives it
def measure(vector):
model = pt.ModelParams.from_preset("pt-v3", **vector)
panel = pt.facts.measure(seed=7, universe=universe, model=model)
scores = pt.evaluate({"mom": spec}, seed=7, universe=universe,
days=126, model=model)
return {"return_pct": scores["mom"].return_pct,
"impact_bps": scores["mom"].impact_bps,
"return_acf1": panel["return_acf1"]}

s = atlas.survey(axes, measure, samples=256)
s.meta["seeds"] = [7] # required before confirm() will run
s.save("edge-survey.json")

# 4. what moves the return?
print(s.sensitivity("return_pct")["correlations"])

# 5. what shape is the effect?
for b in s.profile("momentum_theta", "return_pct", bins=6)["bins"]:
print(round(b["low"], 3), b["n"], b["median"])

# 6. re-measure the finding on seeds the survey never saw
hi = {"momentum_theta": 0.30, "garch_alpha": 0.09,
"market_factor_sigma": 0.016}
lo = {**hi, "momentum_theta": 0.03}
print(s.confirm(hi, lo, measure_with_seed,
seed_blocks=[range(201, 231), range(301, 331)]))
```

OUTPUTILLUSTRATIVE

```
# 2. three of the 256 planned vectors
{'momentum_theta': 0.3184, 'garch_alpha': 0.0412, 'market_factor_sigma': 0.0231}
{'momentum_theta': 0.0721, 'garch_alpha': 0.1103, 'market_factor_sigma': 0.0094}
{'momentum_theta': 0.2075, 'garch_alpha': 0.0688, 'market_factor_sigma': 0.0157}

# 4. ranked by |rho|
{'momentum_theta': 0.7412, 'market_factor_sigma': -0.1883,
'garch_alpha': 0.0417}

# 5. low edge of bin, rows in bin, median return_pct
0.0 43 0.31
0.067 42 0.58
0.133 43 0.94
0.2 42 1.26
0.267 43 1.51
0.333 43 1.74

# 6.
{'outputs': {'return_pct': {'gaps': [1.401, 1.372],
'mean_gap': 1.387, 'sd_gap': 0.021,
'consistent_sign': True,
'reverses_sign': False}},
'seed_blocks': [[201, ...], [301, ...]],
'survey_seeds': [7],
'summary': 'return_pct: candidate above baseline in both blocks, ...'}
```

Read step 4 and step 5 together. momentum_theta dominates at rho 0.74 while the two volatility axes read near zero, and the profile climbs steadily across the range with no flattening. Step 6 confirms it on sixty fresh seeds in two blocks, same sign both times. The figures in that block are illustrative, as the badge says: what is real is the shape of the finding and what you do about it.

So the return is the herding knob. Turn the knob down and the edge goes with it, and real markets have no such knob, which is why this edge will not transfer. An agent whose return stayed flat across those six bins would have passed the strongest robustness test the simulator can give it.

---


# Atlas

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/atlas.html

REFERENCE

# Atlas

Atlas runs your measurement in hundreds of slightly different markets and builds a table of what came out. You then ask the table which model settings your result actually depends on.

This page is Loop A, calibrating the market model. You do not need this to test a strategy. The two loops says which is which.

## What It Does, Step by Step

- You name some model settings and a range for each. Say herding between 0 and 0.4.

- Atlas picks a few hundred combinations spread evenly across those ranges.

- It runs your own measurement function at each one. Your function decides what gets measured: a return, a drawdown you compute yourself, a fill rate, a realism statistic. Anything you can compute from a run.

- You get back a table with one row per combination: settings in, your numbers out.

- Everything else on this page is a question you ask that table. Which setting moved my number, what shape the effect had, and what trade-offs exist.

You measure once and can then ask as many questions as you like, since the table saves to a file.

## How the Points Are Chosen

Evenly, using Latin hypercube sampling. Each range is cut into as many slices as there are points, and every slice gets exactly one point. That matters because a plain random sample leaves gaps and clumps that look like structure when you analyse them. Even coverage is also what makes a few thousand points useful across fifty settings at once. Sampling is seeded, so the same survey reproduces exactly.

## Why Sampling Beats Searching

If you already know which settings matter, run a search. If you do not, a search fails expensively: the optimiser will happily wreck anything your objective does not measure, and you find out afterwards. Six calibration searches on this simulator were rejected in two days, each one revealing a trade the objective had made behind everyone’s back. Anything outside the objective is free for the optimiser to spend.

The other half of the problem was that nobody had measured how the settings move the outputs. Every search was a walk across a room no one had mapped, in a direction someone had guessed at. A survey maps it first. A Pareto front then puts every available trade side by side so a person picks, rather than an optimiser picking quietly.

## The Methods

axes_forname the boxsurveysample itsensitivityprofile, paretoa human picksa vectorconfirmdisjoint seedsgatesthirty seedscontroloverfittingemit_preseta new name

on seeds disjoint from the survey's, or confirm refuses to run
MAP -- screening resolution
PROVE -- full resolution

thenthen
then
thenthen
then

A survey runs at screening resolution, which is enough
to rank and describe and not enough to believe. Everything on the second
row re-measures at full resolution, and the connector is the requirement
confirm enforces: the seed blocks
it is handed must be disjoint from the ones the survey recorded.

MethodQuestion it answers

sensitivity(output)Which parameters move this output, ranked by rank correlation. Curved monotone effects read correctly under ranks; a linear measure would bury them.
profile(param, output)What shape the effect has: monotone, saturating, an interior optimum, nothing. Each bin reports a median with its p10-p90 spread, never a bare mean, because every other parameter is varying inside a bin.
unidentified(outputs)Which parameters move nothing you named, and would waste a search's budget. The threshold tightens as the survey grows.
pareto(objectives)The non-dominated rows over several objectives at once. The method the module exists for.
attribution(a, b, output)Why B beats A, decomposed per changed parameter, with a noise scale beside each contribution.
explain(output) · report_front(...)The findings as prose that carries its own row counts, ranges and caveats inline.
confirm(candidate, baseline, ...)Whether a screening finding survives fresh seeds at full resolution. The check you always run before believing a survey result.

## Reading Each Method's Output

sensitivity returns the correlations inside their provenance, so a number cannot shed its basis:

PYTHON
Copy

```
s.sensitivity("return_pct")
# {"output": "return_pct",
# "correlations": {"momentum_theta": 0.61, ...}, # sorted by |rho|
# "rows_total": 500, "rows_used": 496, "rows_error": 3,
# "rows_nonfinite": 1, "rows_outside_where": 0, "where": None}

s.sensitivity("return_pct", where={"garch_alpha": (0.06, 0.16)})
# the same question, restricted to a region of OTHER parameters
```

A magnitude here ranks influence over the sampled range. It is an ordering, and it says nothing about how much a unit change buys, so quote it as a rank and never as an elasticity.

profile is where decisions usually turn. An interior optimum says ship a tuned value; a monotone slide to the range edge says the mechanism is net harmful here. A rank correlation cannot tell those apart, and the binned marginal can:

PYTHON
Copy

```
s.profile("momentum_theta", "return_pct", bins=12)
# each bin: {"low", "high", "n", "median", "p10", "p90"}
# log axes bin in log space, so bin counts stay near-uniform
```

pareto and report_front lay out every available trade at the same time:

PYTHON
Copy

```
s.pareto({"return_pct": "max", "impact_bps": "min"})
print(s.report_front({"return_pct": "max", "impact_bps": "min"}))
```

attribution decomposes a difference between two vectors across the parameters that differ. It exists because of a specific failure: a candidate was described in a design document as delivering crisis severity "through correlation", which was right for one of its two parameters and backwards for the other. Every number involved was correct. The connecting sentence was invented.

PYTHON
Copy

```
s.attribution(vector_a, vector_b, "return_pct", measured=(y_a, y_b))
# contributions per changed parameter, each with a noise scale;
# contributions inside 2x their noise land in "within_noise"
```

explain and the other prose renderers state the row counts, ranges and dropped-row tally they stand on, with their own caveats inline. A number invites scepticism and a sentence does not, so the sentence has to carry its own.

## The Failure Modes

### Ranges Are the Most Consequential Choice

axes_for defaults to a quarter to four times a preset's shipped value. That is a convention, and it has been wrong here: a 96-core search once concluded there was nothing to find because the best known value of crisis_blend_ramp (6.0, four point three times ship) sat just outside the default ceiling of 5.6. Override any range you have real information about. A parameter that ships at exactly 0.0 has no multiplicative box at all, and Atlas refuses to guess one, because guessing would silently decide what the map can see. Typo'd override names are refused too, since a typo would leave a default box silently in place.

### Attribution Assumes Additivity

Each contribution is a main effect read off a marginal with every other parameter varying. Strong interactions break the assumption: on a purely multiplicative surface attribution can overstate a contribution several-fold, and an interaction between the changed parameters is attributed to neither. Pass measured= whenever you can. It supplies the true endpoint values, and the residual against the decomposition is the only signal that additivity failed. Without it, the summary says so explicitly rather than presenting an unchecked number.

### Why You Re-measure

The refusal to reuse seeds exists because of a real loss. A candidate here was declared shippable on a 13% improvement. Measured on fresh seed blocks, the same gap read +0.1297 where it was found, then −0.0315, +0.0209 and +0.0233 elsewhere, reversing sign once. Discovery and validation had used the same thirty seeds, so re-measuring reproduced the same fluctuation exactly and reported it as confirmation. It tested reproducibility of the measurement, and said nothing about the effect. confirm therefore refuses overlapping seeds outright, refuses a survey with no seed record, and measures both vectors on the same fresh seeds so path noise cancels in the pair. In practice one block gives you a number and several tell you whether it is a property of the model or just of the paths.

## What Atlas Cannot Tell You

- A near-zero sensitivity is evidence of no monotone relationship over the sampled range at this resolution, never proof of inertness. A parameter that acts only in combination, or only past a threshold the sample never crossed, reads the same way. Ask the targeted question with where=.

- A rank correlation ranks influence. It does not measure how much.

- Failed runs are kept, not hidden. A vector whose measurement raises is recorded and skipped, because a parameter region that crashes the model is a fact about the model. Infrastructure failures cluster in expensive corners, so check where the drops are, not just how many.

---


# Scenarios and Crises

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/scenarios.html

GUIDE

# Scenarios and Crises

A scenario is a path you force the economy down: rates walking up, a VIX spike, a contraction. The engine follows it and everything else carries on around it.

## What This Buys You

A decade of history gives you one hiking cycle and maybe one crisis, and you cannot rerun either. Here you run the same market twice, once with the event and once without, on identical noise. The difference is what the event cost you. That answers things a backtest cannot: does the strategy survive rates doubling, and what does a crisis do to your execution cost.

## No Built-In Crises

There is no canned pandemic, war or crash. A ready-made event hides the choices that decide what your test actually means: how high, how fast, and from where. You get three building blocks instead, three shape constructors, and published recipes whose numbers are all anchored to real episodes you can go and check.

PYTHON
Copy

```
from pretium import Scenario

Scenario().hold(vix=45.0) # pin a field at a level
Scenario().ramp("inflation_rate", # walk it over a window
start=0.02, end=0.09, over=60)
Scenario().step("corporate_bond_yield", # jump it on a given day
before=0.05, after=0.08, at=10)

# shape constructors build a whole scenario in one call:
Scenario.rate_shock(start=0.025, end=0.05, over=15)
Scenario.vix_shock(calm=15.0, peak=45.0, at=10, over=30)
```

Pins on one field lie end to end, so a spike, a plateau and a decay compose into one scenario. Check the path before you spend a run on it: Scenario.table(days) prints the day-by-day values.

## Example: A Rate Shock

Walking the rate from 2.5% to 5% while agents hold positions, against the same market with no shock:

PYTHON
Copy

```
shock = pt.Scenario.rate_shock(start=0.025, end=0.05, over=15)
agents = pt.reference_agents(seed=3) # or your own, see The Agent Harness
pt.evaluate(agents, seed=7, universe=universe, days=20, scenario=shock)
```

AgentCalmHikedDelta

buy_and_hold−5.63%−8.76%−3.13
momentum−7.88%−9.74%−1.86
oracle+14.98%+12.99%−1.99

Buy-and-hold is long only, holds through the repricing, and gives up the most. Momentum and the Oracle trade around it and each give up about two points. The sizes belong to the seed: across sim seeds 5 to 9 buy-and-hold gives up 3.0 to 5.0 points every time, while momentum's give-up spans −1.9 to +0.5. Run more than one seed before you quote a size.

## What a VIX Scenario Moves

VIX moves four things at once, which is why pinning it high feels like a crisis rather than turning up a dial:

- Volatility. The market factor's variance chases a target that scales with (VIX/15)². Realised annual volatility: 31% at VIX 5, 37% at 15, 105% at 45, 126% at 65.

- Spreads. Mean quoted spread goes from 11.7 bps at VIX 15 to 21.5 bps at VIX 65, so trading costs more exactly when you least want it to.

- Correlation. Above VIX 25.5 the cross-section blends toward the market factor: mean pairwise correlation reads +0.20 calm, +0.62 at VIX 45, +0.68 at 65. Diversification stops working, the way it does in a real crisis.

- Credit spreads, recomputed at central-bank meetings, so a VIX path also ends up repricing the yield that equities discount off.

Measured: Universe.random(20-25, seed=11) · 120 days · sim seed 3, pinned through the scenario API. Since the 2026-08-26 era boundary VIX also moves a name's own variance, through garch_vix_coupling; before it, VIX sized only the shared factor. These figures straddle the 32.76% on Realism and Limits rather than sitting near it, the calm pins bracketing it and the crisis pins running three to four times higher, because a pinned VIX is not a normal market: the pin drives the factor variance directly, and these runs use a smaller roster over 120 days rather than the certified 40 names over 252. Compare pins against each other, and take the certified number from an unpinned run. The ratio between two pins is NOT the crisis lever the realism page and the release notes quote: that one runs VIX 5 to VIX 65 on the certified roster over 252 days at thirty seeds and reads 6.04x on pt-v12. Three numbers, three measurements.

## Example: A Liquidity Crisis

PYTHON
Copy

```
crisis = pt.Scenario.vix_shock(calm=18.0, peak=80.0, at=20, over=60)

shocked = pt.facts.measure(seed=3, universe=u, days=120, scenario=crisis)
calm = pt.facts.measure(seed=3, universe=u, days=120,
scenario=pt.Scenario("calm").hold(vix=18.0))
print(f"{calm['annualised_vol_pct']:.2f}% calm, "
f"{shocked['annualised_vol_pct']:.2f}% crisis")
# 39.98% calm, 67.68% crisis
```

The peak of 80 is anchored on the VIX's highest close of 2008: 80.86, on 20 November. The recipe docs anchor every number this way, and also say what each recipe does not claim: reproducing a volatility level is not reproducing a crisis. 2008 was a solvency crisis with a frozen money market behind it, and none of that is in this model.

## Comparing With and Without the Event

The scenario and its baseline see identical noise, draw for draw, because macro state never touches the market's random numbers. So the difference between the two runs is the event and nothing else. compare() reports the paired difference and a draw_delta beside it: zero means the two markets saw the same noise, and anything else means the scenario changed the market's structure (a halt, a delisting), which you want surfaced rather than averaged away.

Scenarios reach every entry point: evaluate, tca.analyse, facts.measure and run_many all take scenario=. Does execution cost more when VIX is high? Measured over ten days and twelve seeds: the VIX 45 world costs more in 12 of 12, median shortfall 11.69 bps against 6.06.

TRAPS AND LIMITS

Pinning federal_funds_rate alone does nothing until the first central-bank meeting, around day 45, because equities discount off the corporate bond yield. A short policy-only study measures exactly 0.00% and looks fine. rate_shock moves the whole curve when you want an immediate repricing.

The shape constructors build a whole scenario. Scenario().hold(...).vix_shock(...) reads like chaining and would throw away your holds; the library refuses it by name.

And gap 3 on the realism page: a scenario's size is right on average and unreliable in one run. The steady-state lever, a sustained crisis against a calm market, reads 6.04x here against 6.16x for real markets on the certified roster, which is within two percent; what is not calibrated is the spread around it, so a single run understates how much of its own move was the scenario. Use scenarios to detect breakage, and size a loss across many seeds or not at all.

## A Whole Crisis Study

A whole crisis study. Build the event, look at the path before you spend anything on it, check the question is answerable, then measure what the crisis did to the market, to a strategy and to execution cost. Same seed throughout, so the only difference between the two worlds is the event.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt
from pretium import Scenario, envelope

u = pt.Universe.random(20, seed=11)

# 1. build the event and its control, and LOOK at the path first
crisis = Scenario.vix_shock(calm=18.0, peak=80.0, at=20, over=60)
control = Scenario("calm").hold(vix=18.0)
for row in crisis.table(120)[:25]:
print(row) # day-by-day, before spending a run

# 2. can this market answer the question? magnitude is NOT certified
print(envelope.check(horizon_days=120, scenario_magnitude=False,
statistics=["annualised_vol_pct",
"cross_sectional_corr"]))

# 3. what the crisis did to the MARKET
shocked = pt.facts.measure(seed=3, universe=u, days=120, scenario=crisis)
quiet = pt.facts.measure(seed=3, universe=u, days=120, scenario=control)
shocked["annualised_vol_pct"], quiet["annualised_vol_pct"]
# 82.16% crisis against 61.76% calm
shocked["cross_sectional_corr"] # correlation rises with it

# 4. what it did to a STRATEGY, same seed both sides
spec = pt.StrategySpec.momentum(lookback_days=1.0, top_k=5)
for label, sc in (("calm", control), ("crisis", crisis)):
scores = pt.evaluate({"mom": spec}, seed=3, universe=u,
days=120, scenario=sc)
print(label, scores["mom"].return_pct, scores["mom"].impact_bps)

# 5. what it did to EXECUTION COST
calm_ex = pt.tca.analyse(my_algo, seed=3, universe=u, days=10,
scenario=Scenario().hold(vix=15))
spike_ex = pt.tca.analyse(my_algo, seed=3, universe=u, days=10,
scenario=Scenario().hold(vix=45))
print(calm_ex.shortfall_bps(), spike_ex.shortfall_bps())
# measured with BuyAndHold, seeds 1 to 12:
# median 6.06 bps calm, 11.69 bps at VIX 45
# the crisis world costs more in 12 of 12, paired median +5.62 bps

# 6. repeat across seeds before quoting any size
for s in range(1, 13):
... # one seed is one sample
```

OUTPUTMEASURED

```
{'day': 0, 'vix': 18.0}
{'day': 1, 'vix': 18.0}
...
{'day': 19, 'vix': 18.0}
{'day': 20, 'vix': 80.0}
{'day': 21, 'vix': 78.97}
{'day': 22, 'vix': 77.93}
{'day': 23, 'vix': 76.90}
{'day': 24, 'vix': 75.87}

inside the envelope
- horizon 120d is within the certified 252d, and no named statistic
meets a measured gap
? annualised_vol_pct is in band at the certified horizon (31.4632 in
(15.0, 36.0)) -- but that is a median across 30 seeds; check
`intervals` for the spread before relying on one seed
? cross_sectional_corr is in band at the certified horizon (0.3063 in
(0.08, 0.56)) -- but that is a median across 30 seeds; check
`intervals` for the spread before relying on one seed

(67.68, 39.98) # annualised vol %, crisis against calm
0.6235 # cross-sectional correlation under the crisis

calm -42.9347 11.9232
crisis -56.6869 95.0928

6.06 11.69 # shortfall bps, calm then VIX 45
```

Every line in that block is a measurement on pretium 0.2.0 under pt-v10, the default before 0.3.0, from the code above it and left as measured rather than relabelled. The scenario rows are elided in the middle and rounded to two decimals; nothing else is edited. Note what the path actually does: vix_shock puts the peak on day at and decays it over the window, rather than ramping up to it.

Volatility goes from 40% to 68%, and correlation climbs with it, 0.49 to 0.62. The strategy's drawdown grows, and you can separate the causes: fair value repricing, wider spreads, and a cross-section that stopped diversifying. Execution cost nearly doubles on all twelve seeds, so that result belongs to the regime rather than to one path.

Do not quote one run's sizes as real. The steady-state crisis lever is calibrated on average, 6.04x against a real 6.16x, and the dispersion around it is not (gap 3); the pinned pair above is a different measurement again. Read the direction and the ordering, and take a magnitude from many seeds rather than from this one.

---


# Checkpoints and Forking

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/forking.html

GUIDE

# Checkpoints and Forking

Freeze a market and resume it later, or split it into several futures from one identical state. This is the machinery for asking what a single decision was worth.

## Why You Would Do This

You want to know what one choice cost you, and there is no way to isolate that in a single run. Run a strategy through a crisis and you learn what happened; fork the market the day before the crisis and you learn what would have happened if you had de-risked, on exactly the same tape, with exactly the same noise. The branches share no memory, so nothing you do to one leaks into the other, which is what makes it a controlled experiment rather than two runs that happened to start alike.

It is also how you avoid paying for the same hundred days twice. Reaching day 60 costs whatever it costs; forking from there is close to free.

## Two Tools, and They Are Not Interchangeable

pt.branch(engine, count, universe=, seed=)Forks a running engine in constant time by copying its state, columns and generator position included. Measured at under a millisecond for a sixty-day forty-instrument market, against 2,740 ms to reach the same point by replaying its log. Lives in memory, dies with the process.
pt.CheckpointSerialises the inputs and the order log, so the state survives the process and can be published. Resuming replays the log, so it costs roughly what reaching the state cost the first time.

So: branch when the experiment happens now, Checkpoint when someone else needs to start where you started.

One historical exception to the exactness, because it was live for five releases. Snapshots did not carry the engine's log-volume state until 0.2.0, so a restored engine could trade different volume and print different prices. That state is inert on pt-v1 to pt-v3 and live from pt-v4, and the divergence is reproducible: on 0.1.4 a pt-v4 snapshot restored and re-run does not match the uninterrupted run, where pt-v1 and pt-v3 do. Resume anything checkpointed under 0.1.x on a jump-carrying preset with that in mind.

## Forking a Live Engine

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt

universe = pt.Universe.random(40, seed=7)
engine = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=universe)
engine.run_days(60) # the shared history

# both branches carry the full state, including the RNG position
calm, shocked = pt.branch(engine, 2, universe=universe, seed=42)

shocked.pin_macro(corporate_bond_yield=0.09) # one thing differs
calm.run_days(30)
shocked.run_days(30)

calm_close = calm.bars(grain="day")
shocked_close = shocked.bars(grain="day")
```

universe and seed are required because an engine carries neither: it is built from them and keeps them nowhere. The seed barely matters here, since the generator position is restored over whatever it produced, but the universe does: the columns are positional, so a mismatched roster would attach every value to the wrong instrument. The engine refuses that rather than doing it quietly.

A fork of a custom-model run prices under its parent's coefficients, read off the live engine, so a branch cannot silently revert to the shipped preset.

## Checkpoints That Outlive the Process

PYTHON
Copy

```
cp = pt.Checkpoint.of(engine, universe=universe, seed=42,
label="pre-shock, day 60")

open("day60.json", "w").write(cp.to_json())

# later, or elsewhere, or in someone else's hands:
cp = pt.Checkpoint.from_json(open("day60.json").read())
engine = cp.resume()

# or several futures at once
futures = cp.branch(3)
```

Checkpoint.of takes the universe and the seed for the same reason branch does, and it records them so the checkpoint carries the inputs it will need rather than discovering at resume time that it cannot reproduce anything.

resume(universe=...) lets you restore onto a roster you already hold. It is checked against the recorded fingerprint and refused on a mismatch, because tickers are generated positionally: two universes can share every name and no fundamentals, so comparing names would be checking almost nothing. The error message says what a mismatch would give you, which is right prices and wrong fair values.

## Full Example: What Did De-risking Cost?

Sixty days of shared history, then the same market twice: once holding the book through a rate shock, once cutting exposure the day before it starts. Same seed, same noise, one decision different.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt

universe = pt.Universe.random(40, seed=7)
spec = pt.StrategySpec.momentum(lookback_days=1.0, top_k=5)

# 1. shared history
engine = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=universe)
engine.run_days(60)
print(engine.draws_by_stream()) # the position both branches inherit

# 2. publish the fork point, so the experiment is checkable
cp = pt.Checkpoint.of(engine, universe=universe, seed=42,
label="day 60, pre-shock")
open("day60.json", "w").write(cp.to_json())

# 3. two futures from one state
held, derisked = pt.branch(engine, 2, universe=universe, seed=42)

# 4. the same shock reaches both; only the exposure differs
shock = pt.Scenario.rate_shock(start=0.025, end=0.05, over=15)
for eng, gross in ((held, 1.0), (derisked, 0.4)):
for day in range(30):
shock.apply(eng, day)
eng.run_days(1)

# 5. and the counterfactual is exact, because the noise was identical
print(held.draws_by_stream()["market"] == derisked.draws_by_stream()["market"])
```

OUTPUTILLUSTRATIVE

```
# 1.
{'market': 9360000, 'economy': 1440, 'external': 0}

# 5.
True
```

The last line is the point. Equal market-stream draw counts mean the two branches consumed, and therefore saw, an identical noise sequence, so the difference between their P&Ls is the decision and nothing else. That is a number no backtest can produce, because history only ran once and it ran with your orders in it.

## What Travels, and What Does Not

RNG positionThree numbers per generator stream: state, increment and Box-Muller spare. The count grows as the engine gains streams, and restore reads the era off the LENGTH rather than a version field: nine for the original market, economy and external split, then twelve, fifteen, eighteen and twenty-one as jumps, common volume, news and per-name volume arrived. Twenty-one is where it stands on 0.3.0, seven streams of three. A shorter snapshot restores the streams it carries and leaves the rest where the fresh engine put them, so a checkpoint written before a mechanism existed replays as it did then. A pre-split snapshot carrying three is refused with its era named, because it froze a single-stream market this version cannot continue bit-exactly.
modelThe parent's coefficients. A custom-model checkpoint resumes under the custom model or refuses.
universe · seed · macro · order logEverything a resume needs, which is why they are arguments rather than assumptions.
schemaA checkpoint written by a newer version is refused rather than read partially.

Related: Scenarios and Crises for the macro paths you fork into, and Citing a Result for publishing the fork point alongside the result.

---


# The Agent Harness

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/agents.html

GUIDE

# The Agent Harness

Any object with an act method is an agent. This page is the whole contract with the harness: what it hands you, what you return, and how it scores you.

This page is Loop B, evaluating a strategy against a market that already exists. The preset is a fixed input here. The two loops says which is which.

## The Contract

An agent needs one method: act(obs) receives an Observation and returns a dict of share quantities keyed by ticker, where positive buys, negative sells, and a ticker you omit or set to zero does nothing. There is no base class to inherit and nothing to register, so any object with that method will do.

PYTHON
Copy

```
class MyAgent:
def act(self, obs):
if not obs.is_first_step_of_day: # once a day, correctly
return {}
ticker = obs.tickers[0]
shares = 0.01 * obs.avg_volume(ticker) # size by participation
return {ticker: shares}

scores = pt.evaluate({"mine": MyAgent()}, seed=7,
universe=universe, days=10)
print(scores["mine"].return_pct, scores["mine"].trades)
```

THE TRAP THAT HAS COST PEOPLE REAL RUNS

obs.step counts the whole run, not the day. At the default six steps a day, day 1 starts at step 6 and day 3 at step 18. So if obs.step != 0: return {} reads like a once-a-day guard and is a once-a-run guard: the agent trades on the first step of day zero, never again, and produces a scorecard with trades=1 and no errors. It looks exactly like an agent that considered the market and declined.

Use obs.is_first_step_of_day, obs.is_last_step_of_day or obs.step_of_day. The library cannot catch the mistake, because it is arithmetic on an integer with no call to intercept.

## What You Are Handed

Observation is deliberately narrow: everything on it is something a real trader could see, and nothing on it is something only the simulator knows.

MemberWhat it is

obs.stepIndex over every decision point in the run. Day 1 starts at 6 under the default cadence.
obs.step_of_dayIndex within the day, 0 at every open. Derived, so it cannot disagree with step.
obs.is_first_step_of_dayTrue at the day's opening decision point. The correct once-a-day guard.
obs.is_last_step_of_dayTrue at the day's final decision point, before the close.
obs.dayDay index in the run.
obs.steps_per_dayThe harness cadence. Exposed because an agent reasoning about a horizon cannot infer it at step zero.
obs.tickersThe roster, in index order.
obs.pricesCurrent prices, aligned to tickers.
obs.price(ticker)One price by name.
obs.book(ticker)The live order book, with the depth a trader would see.
obs.avg_volume(ticker)Average daily volume. Public information, and how size should be reasoned about.
obs.participation(ticker, shares)That order as a fraction of average daily volume.
obs.position(ticker)Your current holding, in shares. Zero if none.
obs.portfolioThe Portfolio: cash and positions.
obs.engineThe engine itself. Available, and using it for anything a trader could not see makes your result a different claim.

SIZE IN PARTICIPATION, NOT SHARES

Impact scales with participation. The same 13.7 million shares is 0.05x a day's volume in one name here and 407x in another; the first order moves nothing and the second moves the price 47%. An agent sizing in flat share counts is not choosing a position, it is running a different experiment per instrument.

## The Two Objects You Reach Through

obs.portfolio is a Portfolio: your cash and your holdings.

portfolio.cashUninvested cash.
portfolio.positionsA dict of ticker to Position. A ticker you hold nothing in is absent rather than present at zero, which is why obs.position(ticker) exists.
position.quantityShares held. Negative when short.

obs.book(ticker) returns the live OrderBook, with the depth on each side as PriceLevel entries carrying a price and a size. That is what lets an agent size against real liquidity instead of guessing: walk the levels and you know what your order will actually pay before you send it.

## The Optional Second Method

explain(day) is optional, and returns the factor you believe drove the largest recent move, as one of the nine names in The Nine Components. The harness compares your answer against the engine's own attribution and reports the hit rate as explanation_accuracy on the scorecard.

The signature is explain(self, day), not explain(self). Get it wrong and nothing raises where you will see it: the harness records the error per day and reports explanation_accuracy as None, so the column reads - and looks like the feature is switched off.

PYTHON
Copy

```
class MyAgent:
def act(self, obs):
...

def explain(self, day):
return "momentum" # one of the nine factor names
```

## How the Harness Runs You

pt.evaluate owns the session, and its defaults are the shape of your run, so they matter more than most defaults do.

ArgumentDefaultWhat it does

agents-A dict of name to agent instance or StrategySpec.
seed-The market. Required.
universe-The roster. Required.
days5Trading days to run.
steps_per_day6Decision points per day. The clock advances between them, so a stepped day is bit-identical to one unbroken session.
ticks_per_step65Minutes per step. Six times 65 is the 390-minute day.
cash1_000_000.0Starting cash.
max_leverage2.0Gross exposure cap. Orders that would breach it are rejected and counted in rejected.
macroNoneDay-zero macro state.
scenarioNoneA macro path to impose.
modelNonePreset name or ModelParams. Every agent in one call runs the same model, because scoring across models would compare markets.
start(9, 30, 3)Session start time.

Agents are stateful, and one instance cannot be reused across two calls. Build a fresh instance per evaluation, or pass a factory, as pt.rank does.

No fees or commissions are charged. Everything an order costs you comes from the book: the spread you cross and the levels you consume. Borrow costs are not modelled either, so a short is free to hold.

## What You Get Back

You get one Scorecard per agent, and as_dict() returns every field on it. Note that there is no Sharpe or drawdown here: compute those from bars if you want them.

FieldMeaning

nameThe key you passed in.
pnlProfit and loss in currency.
return_pctReturn as a percentage.
final_net_worthCash plus marked positions at the end.
tradesFills executed.
turnoverTraded notional.
impact_bpsYour footprint against the same seed with nobody trading. Read it over a day or two, not weeks: fills feed back into the price process, so the gap compounds and by day three the sign belongs to the seed.
max_leveragePeak gross exposure reached.
rejectedOrders refused, usually by the leverage cap.
errorsExceptions your agent raised, per step. Check this before reading anything else.
explanationsYour explain answers beside the engine's.
explanation_accuracyShare of days you named the right factor, or None if you did not implement explain.
seed · universe_fingerprintWhich market this came from. A leaderboard without both is a table that cannot be rerun.
strategy_fingerprintSet when the agent came from a StrategySpec. Empty for a hand-written agent, which is the honest reading: that result is reproducible only by citing code at a commit.
model_fingerprintWhich coefficients priced it.

## A Complete Custom Agent

A complete agent that buys the cheapest names against fair value, sizes by participation, rebalances once a day and explains itself, which you can paste and run as it stands.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import pretium as pt

class ValueAgent:
"""Buy the most undervalued names, one decision a day."""

def __init__(self, top_k=5, participation=0.02):
self.top_k = top_k
self.participation = participation

def act(self, obs):
if not obs.is_first_step_of_day:
return {}

# rank by discount to fair value, which a real trader would
# estimate; here we use our own crude proxy: price vs its own
# 5-day mean, held on the agent.
history = getattr(self, "_hist", [])
history.append(list(obs.prices))
self._hist = history[-6:]
if len(self._hist) 1:
orders[ticker] = delta
return orders

def explain(self, day):
return "reversion"

universe = pt.Universe.random(30, seed=11)
scores = pt.evaluate({"value": ValueAgent(),
**{k: v for k, v in pt.reference_agents(seed=3).items()}},
seed=7, universe=universe, days=20)

for name, card in scores.items():
print(f"{name:16s} {card.return_pct:+7.2f}% trades={card.trades:4d} "
f"errors={len(card.errors)} why={card.explanation_accuracy}")
```

OUTPUTMEASURED

```
value -19.99% trades= 5 errors=56 why=0.0
buy_and_hold -5.01% trades= 30 errors=0 why=None
random -2.70% trades=3583 errors=0 why=None
momentum +0.26% trades=1485 errors=0 why=None
mean_reversion +13.44% trades=1606 errors=0 why=None
oracle +15.68% trades=1124 errors=0 why=1.0
```

Measured: pretium 0.3.0, pt-v12, the code above it run verbatim. Nothing is edited, which is the point of the block.

Read errors first, and both failure shapes are in front of you. The QUIET one is a guard bug: a suspiciously low trades count with an EMPTY error list, which is the trap at the top of this page. The LOUD one is the value row here, 5 trades against 56 errors, every one of them trade would take leverage to N above the 2.00x limit. Sizing at 2% of average volume across five names asks for far more than a $1,000,000 account can carry, so the harness rejects the order instead of filling it. That agent is not a bad strategy, it is an unsized one, and its why=0.0 is the same story: it answers "reversion" every day whatever moved. Then remember the oracle reads the true mispricing, so it is a reference rather than a competitor, and one seed ranks the seed as much as the agents. Take it to many markets before you believe an ordering.

# Presets and Custom Models

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/change.html

GUIDE

# Presets and Custom Models

The model's coefficients ship as named presets. You can change any settable coefficient at runtime, and the fingerprint makes sure a changed model can never pass as the shipped one.

This page is Loop A, the coefficients a calibration produces. Loop B cites a preset rather than changing one. The two loops says which is which.

## Reasons to Touch the Model

People change the model for three reasons: they want a calmer or wilder market for a stress study, they are studying the model itself one coefficient at a time, or they are calibrating against their own data. Even if you change nothing, you still quote the preset name, because it is part of what lets someone else rerun your result.

## Presets

A preset names the complete coefficient set, frozen and documented. pt-v12 is the current default, and every earlier preset from pt-v1 to pt-v11 stays selectable and reproduces bit for bit. What that guarantee covers is the PRESET: naming one pins the coefficient set and the market it produces on a given package version, and a run is only fully specified by (package version, model, universe fingerprint, seed). See Install and Versioning for what a package-version change can and cannot move. The reason is comparability: (package version, model, universe fingerprint, seed) is a complete, citable specification of a market. If every user ran a bespoke coefficient set, "tested on the pretium simulator" would mean nothing.

PYTHON
Copy

```
eng = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=u, model="pt-v12") # the default, spelled out
eng = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=u, model="pt-v1") # an earlier era, still exact
```

Twelve presets ship. pt-v12 is the default; the other eleven are selectable by name and none of them has ever been un-shipped.

### How the presets compare, and how each compares to a real market

Real stock markets have habits, and this simulator is measured against 14 of them: how far prices swing over a year, how often a wild day happens, whether a wild day tends to be followed by another one, whether shares fall together harder than they rise together, whether heavy trading shows up alongside big moves, and nine more. Each habit has a range measured from a real US large-cap market between 2015 and 2025. A preset matches a habit when its own measurement lands inside that range, so 14 of 14 means it behaved like a real market on every habit tested. The full list, with every range and every measurement, is on Realism and limits.

The first row is the real market itself. All twelve presets were measured in one run, thirty seeds each, one method throughout, so the rows compare. Ranked best first.

The columns. 1 year and 2 years count habits matched out of 14; the two-year column scores against ranges re-derived for a two-year window, which is a stricter ruler. New roster is one year on a 60-name roster no preset was tuned against. Typical year is annualised volatility, how far prices move over a year. Crisis is how much more violently prices swing in a crisis than in a calm market.

This is a ranking, not a menu. Use the default unless you have a reason not to, and name it either way: the earlier presets are here so a result recorded under one still replays bit for bit, not so you can shop among them. A preset further down this table is not broken, it is earlier.

Showing the top 10 of 12. pt-v2, pt-v1 are still selectable and still reproduce bit for bit; they rank below the rows above on the same measurement, which is why they are not listed rather than because they were withdrawn.

### The 14 habits

Each one is a thing real stock markets are known to do, with the range a real US large-cap market stayed inside between 2015 and 2025. A preset matches a habit when its own measurement lands in that range. The ranges are wide because real markets are: a calm year and a crisis year are both real.

## Custom Models and Fingerprints

PYTHON
Copy

```
custom = pt.ModelParams.from_preset("pt-v1", garch_alpha=0.12)
eng = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=u, model=custom)
eng.model_fingerprint # "custom-7f290e34" -- never "pt-v1"
```

The fingerprint is the first 8 hex characters of a sha256 over the canonical serialisation: names sorted, values as raw IEEE-754 bit patterns. A coefficient set bit-identical to a shipped preset fingerprints as that preset's name. Anything else fingerprints as custom-XXXXXXXX. ModelParams is immutable once built, so a fingerprint someone quoted cannot drift afterwards. The rule is simple: you may change the model, and a changed model has a different name.

The fingerprint travels everywhere a result does: scorecards, manifests, checkpoints, forks, replay. A manifest for a custom-model run embeds the full coefficient dictionary and reproduce() rebuilds that exact market or refuses by name.

## Comparing Presets Fairly

Nothing settable may change how many random draws are taken or in what order. Market hours, the 390-tick day, the calendar and the sector key order are the draw schedule, and a preset changes what the draws are multiplied into, never the schedule. Run the same seed under two models and the draw counts match, so every difference in the outcome is a parameter effect, never reshuffled noise.

## What Is Settable

pt.ModelParams.settable() lists the runtime surface: the two variance processes (per-name GJR-GARCH and the market factor's), the factor sigmas and idiosyncratic scale, the mispricing dynamics, the news and flow coefficients, and the guards in the tick chain. Guards are worst-case guarantees rather than tuning knobs, and a calibration search excludes them.

The rest of the surface, such as fair-value coefficients and the macro chain's constants, is visible in to_dict() and covered by the fingerprint, and overriding it is refused by name: those constants are compile-time in this build, and accepting an override the engine would ignore would make the fingerprint a lie. Two coefficients are derived: mispricing_phi and s_phi_tick come from mispricing_half_life_days and cannot be set directly.

## Example: Calibrating Your Own Market

A model builder wants a market with stronger volatility clustering for a stress study, and wants the result to be citable. The loop: sweep candidate coefficients, score each candidate's realism panel, confirm the pick on fresh seeds, then publish the fingerprint beside the result.

PYTHON
Copy

```
from pretium import facts, loss

for alpha in (0.02, 0.04, 0.08):
params = pt.ModelParams.from_preset("pt-v3", garch_alpha=alpha)
panels = [facts.measure(seed=s, universe=u, model=params)
for s in range(1, 7)]
result = loss.band_distance_loss(panels)
print(params.fingerprint, result["loss"])
```

band_distance_loss prices each statistic's band exit in units of its own seed noise and returns the full per-statistic breakdown with the scalar inside it. The statistics outside the objective ride along in every result as a standing falsification verdict, and stay out of the loss, because an optimiser is only allowed to chase what the project decided it may chase. That is a policy about the search, not a claim that the rows are unreachable: the volume-change row was called unreachable until 0.2.0, pt-v10 held it at one year, and pt-v12 holds it at two -- the gap that named it is retired.

When the sweep has more than a handful of knobs, survey first: Atlas tells you which parameters move your panel before you spend a search on them, and confirm re-measures the winner on seeds the sweep never saw. The library consumes presets and does not ship an optimiser; six consecutive searches on this simulator were rejected for trades a scalar objective made silently, and that history is why.

Ship the result as (package version, custom-XXXXXXXX, universe fingerprint, seed) plus a RunManifest. A reader with the package and the manifest rebuilds your market bit for bit, or is told exactly why not. Citing a Result has the full list and a worked methods paragraph.

## Turning One Knob Down

One coefficient, honestly named, all the way to a citable result. The library's best-known defect is that returns trend (+0.249 autocorrelation at lag one under pt-v1). One knob controls it, and turning it down is a two-line experiment:

PYTHON
Copy

```
custom = pt.ModelParams.from_preset("pt-v1", momentum_theta=0.05)
custom.fingerprint # "custom-..." -- never "pt-v1"

eng = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=u, model=custom)
panel = pt.facts.measure(seed=1, universe=u, model=custom)
panel["return_acf1"]
# measured for this counterfactual: +0.034, inside the real band
# (-0.08, 0.06), where pt-v1 reads +0.249. Volatility and kurtosis
# essentially unchanged. Measured on an earlier model era; re-measure
# before leaning on it.

manifest = pt.RunManifest.of(eng, seed=42, universe=u)
open("run.json", "w").write(manifest.to_json())
```

The pieces working together: the coefficient set is immutable, the fingerprint says loudly that this is not the shipped model, the panel re-measures realism under it instead of inheriting the certificate, and the manifest hands a reader everything needed to rebuild the exact market and check you.

---


# MCP Server for Market Simulation

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/mcp.html

CONNECT

# The MCP Server

pretium ships an MCP server, so a coding agent can drive the simulator through tool calls instead of Python. You ask in plain English: does a momentum strategy beat buy-and-hold here, and is the difference real?

## Install and Register

SHELL
Copy

```
pip install "pretium[mcp]"
claude mcp add pretium -- pretium-mcp
```

Or in a client's config file:

JSON
Copy

```
{"mcpServers": {"pretium": {"command": "pretium-mcp"}}}
```

It takes no arguments and speaks MCP over stdio.

## The Tools

Eleven, all read-only. Seven answer a question directly, two compose an input as data, and two run past what a conversation can wait for.

ToolWhat it answers

describe_simulator()What this is, what it reproduces, what it cannot do. Call it first.
check_envelope(horizon_days, statistics=[], sector_concentrated=false, scenario_magnitude=false)Is my question inside the certified range, before I spend anything on it?
validate_strategy(spec)Is this spec well-formed, and what is its fingerprint?
evaluate_strategies(strategies, seed, days, universe_size=…, universe_seed=…, preset=…)How do these do on one identical market?
rank_strategies(strategies, seeds, days, universe_size=…, universe_seed=…, preset=…)Which is really better, across seeds, with a paired sign test?
run_stress_scenario(kind, strategies, seed, days, …)What a rate, VIX or volatility shock does, always against its own unshocked control. kind is one of rate, vix or vol.
explain_price_move(seed, day, ticker, …)Why a price moved: the nine components that sum to it.
build_universe(size=40, seed=111, sectors=None, instruments=None, limit=20)Build a roster and preview it in one call, generated from size and seed with optional sector concentration, or from explicit instruments. Returns a universe document the run tools take, so a roster is composed once and reused rather than re-specified per call. A sector-concentrated roster is one of the five named envelope gaps, and this is what makes it askable.
build_scenario(steps, label="", ...)Compose a macro path as data from a list of steps, the same grammar the Python surface uses. Returns a scenario document the run tools accept.
start_job(tool, arguments={})Run one of the expensive tools in the background. This is how you reach the certified 252-day horizon, which a direct call cannot finish inside a conversation.
check_job(job_id=None)Poll a background run and collect its result. With no id, reports every job.

## Sending a Strategy

You cannot send Python to the server. A tool call cannot carry a function, and accepting code as a string would turn this into a remote-code-execution endpoint with a market simulator bolted on. So the server speaks StrategySpec documents, the same declarative grammar that makes a result citable. The full grammar, every signal.kind and every default is in Tables and Schemas.

JSON
Copy

```
{
"signal": {"kind": "momentum", "lookback_days": 1.0},
"portfolio": {"top_k": 5, "gross": 1.0}
}
```

One thing works differently here than in the library: if spec_version is missing, the server fills it in. Models writing a spec mid-conversation leave it out every time, and rejecting them for it wastes a round trip. If a spec does name a version, that version is kept, so anything newer than the build is still refused.

What the grammar cannot express: path dependence, conditional logic, custom signals. Those need a Python agent, and Running a Market is where that lives.

## Every Result Carries Its Own Caveats

When you call pt.evaluate yourself, you have the docstrings and this site to hand. A model calling evaluate_strategies has the tool result and nothing else, and it will then summarise that result for someone with even less. Hand it {"return_pct": 88.7} and it will say the strategy made 88.7%.

So every result carries a caveats list beside its numbers. Two properties are worth knowing about.

### Earned per Call

Each one fires on something about the call you actually made. A multi-seed run does not get the single-seed warning. A strategy with no momentum in it hears nothing about return autocorrelation. In practice, warnings that never change get skipped.

### Computed at Call Time

Every number in them is read from the published realism figures when the tool runs, so a warning cannot go stale while the model it describes moves on.

WHY COMPUTED, AND NOT HARDCODED

While this server was being written, PRODUCT.md and README.md were both found still asserting a return autocorrelation of +0.219 and +0.249, from a superseded preset. The default has moved twice since that was written, from pt-v3 to pt-v10 at 0.2.0 and on to pt-v12 at 0.3.0, which certifies 0.0239: comfortably inside the real-market band of −0.08 to 0.06, and about a tenth of either quoted figure. This server never types that number. It reads it out of envelope.CERTIFIED on every call, so the sentence moves when the preset moves.

A hardcoded caveat is how a caveat becomes false, and a false caveat told to a model is worse than none.

SAMPLE OUTPUTILLUSTRATIVE

```
{
"results": {"momentum": {"return_pct": 88.7, "sharpe": 1.94, ...}},
"seed": 42,
"days": 5,
"caveats": [
"SINGLE SEED: one market is one sample. This result measures the
seed as much as the strategy. Use rank_strategies across seeds
before stating which is better.",
"SHORT WINDOW: 5 days. The statistics that make this market
credible are 252-day measurements, so this run is a sample of
the market rather than a description of it.",
"This strategy trades a return-continuation or reversal signal,
so its edge depends on the simulator's return autocorrelation:
return_acf1 measures 0.0239 against a real-market band of
-0.08 to 0.06 (in band) at the certified 252-day horizon.",
"NOT A FORECAST: simulated performance does not predict live
returns. Read this as a stress test."
]
}
```

If a summary drops the caveats, it is misreporting the result.

## Seeds, and How Many

evaluate_strategies runs one market. It is fast and a fine first look, but a verdict from one seed is measuring the seed as much as the strategy.

rank_strategies is the honest version. It runs many seeds and reports paired_sign_tests, where both entrants traded the same market on each seed. Pairing them takes the market out of the comparison.

Quote pooled_capture, not seeds_first. The latter counts league positions among all entrants and splits arbitrarily on a tie. Try submitting a momentum spec against the momentum baseline: it comes back all ties, zero paired seeds. That is right, because they are the same strategy. A league table would have picked a winner on a coin flip.

## Limits, and Why

LimitValue

max_days60
max_universe120
max_strategies8
max_seeds12

These are about wall-clock time and the library itself imposes none of them. Forty names with the baselines takes roughly 0.5s at 5 days, 20s at 60, and 95s at 252, and a tool call has to come back while someone is still waiting.

That last number is why max_days stops short of the tested 252-day horizon on a direct call, and why every scored result gets a SHORT WINDOW warning. The statistics that make this market believable were measured over a year, so a five-day run samples the market rather than describing it. When you need the full horizon, use start_job and check_job: the run happens in the background and the conversation collects it afterwards.

## What the Server Leaves Out

- Atlas. A survey is thousands of simulations and takes hours, so nothing useful could come back from it inside a conversation. Run it from Python.

- The 87 model coefficients. You pick presets by name. Coefficients made up on the fly give you a market nobody calibrated, reported as though it were a shipped one.

- Writes. Every tool is read-only and pure: same arguments, same bytes, every platform.

Related: Realism and Limits is where the caveats come from, Tables and Schemas has the spec grammar, Running and Evaluating has the evaluation API, and Running a Market is the library underneath.

---


# An LLM Agent

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/llm-agent.html

CONNECT

# An LLM Agent

A worked example, not a library feature: examples/08-claude-agent.py defines a ClaudeTrader that implements the same agent protocol as anything else, and the harness scores it against the reference agents. Nothing in the library is Claude-aware, so any provider that returns structured output slots in the same way.

SHELL
Copy

```
pip install "pretium[claude]"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # or: ant auth login
python examples/08-claude-agent.py
```

The interesting part is not that a language model can pick a portfolio. It is that this harness can check whether it picked one for the right reason.

## The Second Score

Every agent gets a P&L. An agent that also implements explain(day) gets a second score on top: the harness compares the factor the agent blames for the day against the engine's own record of what actually moved prices.

OUTPUTMIXED, SEE NOTE

```
agent pnl impact why-right
oracle 229751 ... 100%
claude ... ... ..%
momentum 21520 ... -
```

The oracle and momentum rows are measured, by the same call the example makes: pt.reference_agents(seed=3) over Universe.random(12, seed=7), seed 2026, 20 days, max_leverage=2.0. The claude row is blank on purpose. Every run costs money, no published run exists yet, and one seed would not be worth quoting anyway. Run it and you get your own numbers.

The oracle scores 100% on why-right because it reads the true mispricing directly, which is also why it is a reference rather than a competitor.

A model can earn a good P&L by accident, and the second score is the one no real market can produce, because attributing a real price move to mean reversion rather than order flow is exactly the thing nobody can do. So the run gets at whether the model is describing the mechanism or telling a plausible story.

## How It Is Wired

Claude returns a structured decision, so nothing has to be parsed out of free text.

PYTHON
Copy

```
class Decision(BaseModel):
weights: dict[str, float] # -1.0 to 1.0 per ticker
driver: Factor # one of the engine's nine factors
reasoning: str

response = self.client.messages.parse(
model="claude-opus-5",
max_tokens=4000,
system=[{"type": "text", "text": SYSTEM,
"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
output_config={"effort": self.effort},
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": self._prompt(obs)}],
output_format=Decision,
)
```

driver is a literal of the nine components, so the answer comes from a closed set and can be checked against the truth table. messages.parse validates the response against the schema.

The market's rules go in the system prompt and never change, so they carry a cache breakpoint. The volatile part, prices and positions and the book, goes in the user turn after it. Put the market state in the system prompt and you invalidate the cache on every call.

The model returns weights rather than share counts, and the example converts them itself: divide by price, cap against average daily volume, difference against the current position. That is a few lines in the agent, and asking a model to do the arithmetic instead adds a place for it to go wrong. There is no library helper for it, because act is specified in shares (see The Agent Harness).

## Known Traps

The harness steps six times a day. steps_per_day defaults to 6, so an agent that calls the API inside act without gating makes six calls a day and six times the bill. The example tracks the last day it acted on:

PYTHON
Copy

```
if obs.day == self._last_day:
return {}
self._last_day = obs.day

# equivalent, and preferred in new code:
# if not obs.is_first_step_of_day:
# return {}
```

Those two are the same guard. obs.is_first_step_of_day is the one to reach for, because it cannot be confused with a once-a-run guard; the day-tracking version is what the example happens to use and works identically.

explain takes the day. The full contract is on The Agent Harness. The signature is explain(self, day), not explain(self). Getting it wrong raises nowhere you will notice: the harness records the error per day and reports explanation_accuracy as None, so the column reads - and looks like the feature is switched off.

## Cost

One call per day, one day per decision. The default run is 20 days over 12 instruments, so 20 calls, which lands around $0.30 to $0.60 at Opus 5 rates with the system prompt cached. It scales linearly with days.

The mechanism does not need a frontier model to demonstrate. Pass model="claude-haiku-4-5" for a cheap smoke test and expect worse answers, particularly on driver.

## What This Does Not Tell You

The same warning as everywhere else on this site, and it applies harder to a language model than to a coded strategy. This market has knowable structure, and the system prompt describes it. Under pt-v3 the residual trend in returns is small enough to sit inside the real-market band (+0.0375 against −0.08 to 0.06), but it comes from a herding coefficient that real markets do not have, and earlier presets ran it four times harder. A model that finds that dial and leans on it is exploiting the simulator rather than showing skill that transfers. If you run under an older preset, check what the prompt is telling it.

The why-right column is the more durable of the two scores, because naming the mechanism correctly is a claim about reasoning rather than about this market's quirks. Even then, run it across seeds before concluding anything, because on one market you are largely ranking the market.

Related: The MCP Server points a model at the simulator the other way round, and Realism and Limits is the warning above, measured.

---


# Running in the Browser

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/wasm.html

CONNECT

# Running in the Browser

pretium compiles to WebAssembly, and the browser build produces bit-identical results to the native one. So you can put a market in a web page and every viewer gets the same market you did.

## A Permalink That Reproduces Exactly

This is what the browser build is for. A URL carrying the seed, the roster and the parameters gives every viewer the same market, on any machine, in any browser. A worked example becomes something a reader can verify rather than take on trust, and a daily challenge becomes a fair contest because everyone is trading the identical tape.

That only works if the browser agrees with the reference implementation to the last bit, which is the measurement below.

## Measured: Identical Digests

One fixed simulation, hashed, from both builds:

OUTPUTMEASURED

```
PYTHON (native macos-arm64) 2b2f314181bde90a9ccabbc8232b03cba2e04221bee85501ffc78ae042cfd8f5
WASM (wasm32-unknown-unknown) 2b2f314181bde90a9ccabbc8232b03cba2e04221bee85501ffc78ae042cfd8f5
```

## Calling It From JavaScript

The build emits a JavaScript module. This is the parity check that ships in tools/wasm/check.mjs, which is also the shortest useful example:

JAVASCRIPT
Copy

```
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
const pt = require(`${process.cwd()}/dist/wasm/pretium.js`);

pt.version(); // the crate version
pt.preset_names(); // ["pt-v1", "pt-v2", ...]

// one fixed simulation, hashed:
// (instruments, universeSeed, simSeed, days, ticksPerStep, preset)
const digest = pt.priceDigest(12, 7, 3, 5, 65, 'pt-v3');
```

Both surfaces call one core function, engine::fixed_simulation_digest, so the check compares implementations of the engine rather than two harnesses that would then have to be kept in step themselves. The Python side of the same comparison is tests/test_wasm_parity.py.

Types come free if you want them: wasm-bindgen emits a .d.ts alongside the module, so TypeScript consumers get the signatures without anything extra. Nothing in the shipped tooling is TypeScript.

## Size

raw204,290 bytes
gzipped72,981 bytes
brotli60,285 bytes

About 200 KiB raw and 71 KiB gzipped, for a whole market simulator with an order book in it. Measured on the 0.3.0 artefact tools/wasm/build.sh produces: the script prints the raw and gzip figures itself, and the brotli line is brotli -q 11 over the same file.

## Building It

SHELL
Copy

```
tools/wasm/build.sh
```

One command: it builds, runs wasm-bindgen, and verifies the digest. A build whose digest does not match fails there rather than in someone's browser.

## Why This Is Possible Here

Most simulators cannot offer a deterministic browser build. Two things make it work here.

WebAssembly specifies IEEE-754 exactly for add, subtract, multiply, divide and square root, so the arithmetic is pinned by the spec rather than by the engine you happen to be running.

And this crate ships its own exp, log, sin and cos rather than calling the platform maths library, which is the usual reason a browser build disagrees with a native one. The same decision that buys cross-platform identity on the desktop is what buys it in the browser. See Under the Hood for the measurement behind that.

## Where It Is Still Loose

Two caveats, stated rather than folded into a blanket determinism claim.

- NaN payload bits are not specified by wasm. The digest refuses to hash a non-finite value, so if one appears you get a visible failure instead of a match that quietly means nothing.

- Relaxed SIMD is non-deterministic by design. It is off by default and it has to stay off.

## What wasm32-unknown-unknown Means

Readers ask, so: in <arch>-<vendor>-<os> both unknowns are literal. There is no filesystem, no sockets, no clock, no threads, no environment and no process. pretium is unaffected because its only dependencies are libm and sha2, neither of which wants any of that.

One practical note if you are integrating it: a Rust panic reaches JavaScript as RuntimeError: unreachable executed with no message attached, so install console_error_panic_hook before you spend an afternoon on a blank error.

## One Implementation, Two Surfaces

The day loop lives in the core, so the browser and Python surfaces run the same code rather than two copies of it. Under the Hood has the design rule behind that, and why a binding that re-implements a modelling decision is a fork wearing the costume of glue code.

---


# Real Companies from EDGAR

Source: https://simoncoombes.github.io/pretium/edgar.html

CONNECT

# Real Companies from EDGAR

Seed a universe from real SEC filings. The fundamentals are real; every price path stays synthetic.

## When Real Fundamentals Help

A generated universe is plausible but far too tidy. Real filings are messy in useful ways: valuations spread properly, sector weights are lopsided, and loss-makers turn up in realistic numbers. If your strategy reads fundamentals, test it on this.

PYTHON
Copy

```
snap = pt.edgar.fetch(as_of="2024-06-30", limit=100,
user_agent="Jane Roe jane@example.org")
snap.save("edgar-2024h1.json") # the artifact: hashed, citable

universe = pt.Universe.from_edgar(snap, federal_funds_rate=0.03)
engine = pt.Engine(seed=42, universe=universe)
```

## How It Works

- The fetch uses EDGAR's XBRL frames API: five market-wide requests plus one per company kept. It takes a transport argument, so the whole derivation is testable without a network.

- user_agent is required and must carry a contact address. The SEC's fair-access policy asks for one, and the library will not send a made-up one for you.

- Each kept company becomes an Instrument with its filed fundamentals: eps, book value, shares outstanding, and the rest. The model then values and prices those fundamentals under the rate you pass, the same way it does for a generated roster.

## Save and Cite the Snapshot

Companies amend their filings, so the same request will return different numbers next year. The snapshot file is what you cite: hashed, saveable, and enough to rebuild the exact same universe later. Cite the file, not the query.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT GIVE YOU

EDGAR carries no market capitalisation, so limit= ranks companies by shareholders' equity and the roster ends up skewed toward balance-sheet-heavy names rather than resembling a cap-weighted index.

And it loads fundamentals, not behaviour. A loaded ticker is a stock with that company's fundamentals under this model's assumptions. It is not that company: not its real volatility, not its microstructure, not its news flow.

## From Filings to an Archived Result

The whole thing end to end. Fetch the filings, save the snapshot, look at what you got, measure realism on your own roster rather than borrowing the published numbers, run the strategy, then archive it so someone else can rebuild it.

PYTHON
Copy

```
import collections
import pretium as pt
from pretium import envelope

# 1. fetch once, save the artifact, and cite THAT
snap = pt.edgar.fetch(as_of="2024-06-30", limit=60,
user_agent="Jane Roe jane@example.org")
snap.save("edgar-2024h1.json") # hashed, citable, replayable

# 2. build the universe and look at what you actually got
universe = pt.Universe.from_edgar(snap, federal_funds_rate=0.03)
print(len(universe), universe.fingerprint)
print(collections.Counter(i.sector for i in universe)) # NOT balanced
print(sum(1 for i in universe if i.eps
OUTPUTILLUSTRATIVE

```

'Health Care': 7, 'Technology': 6, 'Utilities': 5, ...})

Step 4 refuses, which is the right answer here. Use the panel from step 3 as the realism record for this roster. The published numbers describe a different roster. The sector counts in step 2 are usually why yours differ: 14 financials against a round-robin roster's 3 or 4 per sector changes what the market does. Step 4's two counts are out of the ten-statistic panel of the pt-v3 era and have not been re-measured since; what they establish is a property of the roster rather than of a preset.

Store the snapshot file and the universe fingerprint alongside your results. Re-running the same EDGAR query later gives different numbers, and a re-ordered roster gives a different market.
